subsubtopic: PROMOTION OF SAFETY IN THE WORKPLACE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, June 18 to 24 marks Occupational Health and Safety Week. This year's theme is "Safety Takes Teamwork". In this effort the Canada Safety Council, the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety and the Canadian Standards Association have joined forces to promote safety in the workplace. In doing so they help to promote safety awareness among Canadian business, industry and government.
Notable advances in occupational health and safety have occurred in Canada over the past decade. The inception of the Workplace Hazardous Material Information System by governments throughout the country ensures access to data and instruction on how to handle dangerous material by workers. The creation of the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety in 1978 was also a positive step. The Centre gives access to information regarding hazards in the workplace.
Despite these efforts the rate of accidents in the Canadian workplace is still substantially high. However, we must continue to build on these improvements so that some day all Canadians can work in a healthy and safe environment.

Mr. Speaker, last week on two separate occasions I rose in the House to advise you of some very positive investments taking place as a result of good government policy. One investment was in the pharmaceutical industry in Whitby and the second was in food processing in Trenton. I would like to inform you that another company has just opened a new 50,000 square foot plant in the town of Pickering employing some 50 people.
A British company, David Brown Gear Industries, required a new distribution facility for its products in Canada and wanted to open a warehouse as well in the United States. For your information, Mr. Speaker, I have paraphrased the comments of Mr. Brown, the Chairman of the Board, at the opening ceremonies of the new facility in Pickering. He said, although we had planned to open a new facility in both Canada and the United States, because of the Free Trade Agreement we decided to take advantage of the opportunity provided by the FTA and built a larger facility in Pickering.
He also advised me that because of the healthy economic environment for business in Canada they may also open a manufacturing facility here in Canada. It is encouraging to see the results of good Conservative policies creating jobs in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this coming Friday morning at ten o'clock the ceremonial guard will perform the changing of the guard on Parliament Hill. Today in Ottawa over the lunch hour the Dominion Carilloneur provided a traditional salute to the Canadian Forces.
On behalf of my colleagues and my constituents from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception I wish to convey our

June 21, 1989
thanks and appreciation to the men and women in uniform of the Canadian Forces for the professional and effective way in which they continue to maintain Canada's safety, sovereignty and security, and for working so successfully with our allies to maintain global peace. I would also like to include our DND civilians whose dedication and support are fundamental and essential to the success of the Canadian Forces.
Armed Forces Day will be observed this year on Saturday, June 24, and many Canadian Forces bases will be open to the public. I encourage everyone to visit our military and meet the men and women of the Canadian Forces who serve us so well.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Vancouver Quadra):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Vancouver's Needle Exchange Program is a courageous initiative by Mayor Gordon Campbell and Vancouver City Council. The program not only provides drug users with clean syringes, but it dispenses educational literature, condoms, advice on safe sexual practices and materials to clean syringes.
The program is working. The response rate from drug users is six times higher than expected. No new people are known to have started taking drugs as a result of the program. Indeed, the opposite has happened; people have started seeking help for their drug problems and the program has undercut the black market for drug paraphernalia.
The federal Government has so far refused to provide financial assistance to Vancouver for the program. That is wrong, and I have already written to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty) to tell him so. I understand some Canadians' prudish attitudes, but we have a crisis on our hands. AIDS causes pernicious pneumonia, cancer, wasting syndrome, brain lesions, seizures, spasms and death.
We are long overdue for a national strategy to help prevent the spread of AIDS and to treat people living with AIDS with dignity. Vancouver's Needle Exchange Program is exemplary. I urge the federal Government to begin to provide funding for that program. This is not just a municipal issue or a Vancouver issue, this is a national and international tragedy and it is about time that the Minister of National Health and Welfare got off his butt and responded to the situation.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian ambassador to China has returned to tell the story of its Government's war against its youth, a story made more compelling by the personal pain of his experience. Yet he suggested that economic sanctions directed against that country would be ineffective because of the size and the essential economic autonomy of China.
Will the Canadian people accept this so-called conclusion of such a rational analysis? Does the power and size of a nation provide for a contemptible government immunity from tangible expressions of international contempt? Should Canada and the International Community of Nations be bullied into apparent acquiescence
June 21, 1989

to infamy? I think not. I believe the Canadian people think not.
I pray that the Canadian Government will think not and that for Canada and China it will not be business as usual.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to impress upon the House and on my hon. colleagues the importance of the plant breeders' rights legislation. Canada is one of the very few agriculturally developed countries that does not have a legal mechanism to protect the inventors of new varieties of plants.
Consequently, Canadian research is left to universities and government agencies rather than the private sector. This situation puts Canada far behind most developed countries. In order to compete on the world market, Canadian farmers require hardy, high-producing plants that are disease and pest resistant.
The realization of plant breeders' rights would enable Canadian farmers to compete in global markets. I would like to add that consumers will also benefit from lower prices. I urge my colleagues to support this important legislation.

subsubtopic: CMHC FUNDING FOR PRINCE CHARLES PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are seeing attempts by government Ministers to play down at least four donations totalling $4,800 made to the PC Fund and to two Conservative ridings, including that of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) from moneys laundered by Patricia Starr from CMHC guaranteed funds.

The source of some of these funds, which the Minister of Housing (Mr. Redway) has confirmed in this House on Monday, included CMHC guaranteed funds meant to be used for consulting fees on the Prince Charles housing project.
As neither the Minister of Employment and Immigration, nor the Minister of Housing understands the seriousness of this matter, I call on the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to realize that the integrity, not only of the public contracting system, but that of his Government is at stake, and for the Prime Minister to ask for an open investigation into the involvement of the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the use of CMHC funds in the Prince Charles project in Toronto.

Mr. Speaker, the Soviet Union and the United States are taking a small step towards disarming the seas. They will be sending warships to each other's ports which will be disarmed of their nuclear capacity.
Two weeks ago, the Neptune report, released by Greenpeace, demonstrated the absolute insanity of arming our seas with nuclear weapons and nuclear powered vessels. The report demonstrates that since 1956 there were nine nuclear reactors and 50 nuclear warheads lost on the ocean floor as a result of accidents at sea. Many more accidents and fires involving nuclear material have also occurred.
On June 8, 1989, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) stood in this Chamber and stated: "When there are nuclear weapons there are going to be accidents". There is only one answer. Let us prevent
accidents by preventing nuclear weapons in Canadian waters.
I call on this Government to follow the example of New Zealand and ban all vessels with nuclear capability from Canadian ports.

Mr. Speaker, no mission is more challenging or important to the Members of this House than is the building of our country in unity and in harmony within the concept of diversity as represented by our two official languages and our several cultural origins.
No province has demonstrated more successfully the spirit of humanity, tolerance and goodwill that is the essence of this unique Canadianism, than has my own Province of New Brunswick over the past many years.
Therefore, I take particular pride in the results of a poll released yesterday that reflect clear and continuing support by the large majority of New Brunswickers for the fair application of Canada's policies of bilingualism. I would respectfully urge all of the provinces of our nation to pursue the principles of respect for minority rights which have long characterized the quality of life in New Brunswick.
Canadian unity, with every province at the table, is the goal we must all seek. Nothing less will ever suit, as our heritage to future generations of this country.

subsubtopic: THE NEW SALES TAX-PREVIOUS STATEMENTS BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like the Minister of Finance to explain to me why, in answer to my question yesterday, he denied saying two years ago that he was considering imposing only a federal sales tax, although that is just what he said in his speech to the House of Commons two years ago.

Why did he say two years ago that with a sales tax that excluded the provinces, the hidden tax would disappear, when he tells us today that he does not have the constitutional power without the provinces' agreement?

subsubtopic: THE NEW SALES TAX-PREVIOUS STATEMENTS BY MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in June of 1987, the White Paper that we published set out three proposals. One proposal was a national sales tax which would involve the provinces, a federal-provincial sales tax. That was the objective which we have been working towards up until just before this last Budget.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to let the Minister get away with this because here is what he said. Yesterday he claimed that his reason for misleading Canadians two years ago was that all along he assumed that the provinces would be part of a sales tax proposal. Two years ago in the House of Commons on June 18, 1987 this is what he said:
Ttvo federal-only sales taxes are also being considered: a Goods and Services Tax and a Value-Added Tkx. Sales tax reform will eliminate the hidden tax in the prices consumers pay.
Why, yesterday in the House of Commons, did he misrepresent what he said in the House of Commons two years ago. Why did he not know then when he proposed two federal-only taxes that he did not have the constitutional powers he now maintains will force retailers that ascribe the tax to add the tax to the sales slip?

Mr. Speaker, let me give it to the Leader of the Opposition very clearly. Our proposal is to replace a 13.5 per cent tax which is buried deep in the production process. By the time it reaches the retail level, nobody in this country can tell just what the precise retail tax impact is.
Let me give the Hon. Member some examples from the White Paper of June 18, 1987. For household furniture there was a variation of five points between the high effective tax rate at the retail and the lowest
Oral Questions
effective tax rate. For kitchen utensils, seven points; for garbage bags and paper plates, six and a half points; for lubricating oil and grease it is a seven and a half point spread.
The point that I am making is with the new tax it will be the same for all products across the board that are taxable. That is why I say that this tax is very clear. It is very visible for the consumer whereas with the old tax one could not tell because of that huge spread between the high effective rate and the low effective rate.

Once again I ask the Minister to explain why he has changed his mind. Why did he disguise the true situation to Canadians and why he is now welshing once again on a promise he made to Canadians two years ago?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Immigration. It concerns the deteriorating situation in China.
Earlier today we were all shocked and dismayed to learn that three students were the first to be executed by the Chinese Government for their role in the demonstrations. Moreover, our Canadian Ambassador to China yesterday informed the External Affairs Committee that in reference to Chinese students in Canada, and I quote:
I'd keep a very low profile. The struggle is important but don't get yourself photographed.
Since a policy of ruthless revenge seems to be the response of the Chinese Government, and since Chinese authorities in Canada are monitoring and pursuing the actions of Chinese students on Canadian soil, I ask the Minister rather than simply extending the student visas of these students, is the Government prepared to establish a special program that would allow these students to
make application directly for landed immigrant status in our country?

I think at this stage that we are doing everything we can on behalf of Chinese citizens in Canada and we will continue to do so.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
The disaster facing thousands of people in southwestern Nova Scotia is now more real with the proposal put forth yesterday by the Minister's advisers which virtually shuts down the whole industry by next Thursday for the rest of the year.
The Minister has been warned by the inshore alliance, the Minister's advisers, and others that the consequences of closing down the inshore fishery will be unprecedented hardships on the communities. I therefore ask the Minister to review his policy before the people choose desperate means to protect their livelihoods.
Will the Minister intervene and do something? Will he perhaps listen to the people of these many communities of southern Nova Scotia?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I am certainly as concerned about the plight of the communities of southwestern Nova Scotia as I am of those in all of Atlantic Canada, the problem we are facing this year is one of sustaining the fishery for the long-term future.
It is a fact that the quotas in the Scotia Fundy region have been declining persistently each year over the past decade because more fish have been taken from the water each year than our regulations have provided for. If we are to sustain that fishery and manage it in an
orderly way for the long term, we must also manage the quotas. I would discourage anyone who might consider fishing in excess of these quotas when the inevitable closures do occur.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. With the offshore fishing on Brown's Banks in the very waters of Scotia Fundy to which the Minister just referred, at a time when the inshore fishermen are not allowed to go in these waters adjacent to the coast, and the fishermen know that there are lots of fish. They just have to look at the catches that are now being caught. The Government is again supporting big corporate interests over the many concerns of the communities across the Province of Nova Scotia.
Will the Minister now review the quota management system that he has used for the last five years, a system with many injustices? Will he review it and at least set up a new policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to point out that the inshore fishery of southwestern Nova Scotia is not being closed down.
In fact, 2,300 of the licensed fishermen in the inshore fishery who fish with fixed gear, gill-nets and long line, will be able to fish through the entire season, and 250 of the larger draggers that have grown and replaced small boats with larger vessels over the last several years will be closed down, because they have already caught more fish by this time this year than they caught by this time last year and they have exceeded their quota.
The comments about the offshore sector are superfluous because they relate to an enterprise allocation scheme which the Hon. Member's Government enacted following the Kirby task force in 1983, something which was confirmed and renewed with the advice of all Atlantic fisheries Ministers and the industry in support of those initiatives.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture and concerns the crisis in the Canadian dairy industry.
June 21, 1989

Last summer the Government adopted a new formula for setting the target price for industrial milk. This formula provided for no indexation for input costs such as rising costs for interest rates and fuel. In the new dairy year starting August 1,1 wonder if the Minister will put in place an indexation mechanism to compensate farmers for input costs.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I noticed that the Hon. Member is convening a meeting to discuss the crisis in the dairy industry. I think the crisis in the dairy industry is in the mind of the Hon. Member.
The fact is that last August and again in February, if we were to have stuck to the formula, there would have been a reduction in the target price for industrial milk. The Government, giving due consideration to the fact that there may be an increase in input costs, agreed to waive the cost of production formula and indeed maintain the price at the current level, notwithstanding the fact that it should have been reduced by $1.89 in August and 14 cents in February. I think that shows the kind of flexibility that is generous and compassionate with the dairy farmers, and we intend to continue that way.
On another point, I have indicated to the dairy farmers of Canada that this particular issue, the cost of production formula indexation, the issue of the trade negotiations and discussions with regard to the renewal of the five-year dairy plan, are things that I am prepared to discuss with them in a formalized way under a proposition which we would refer to as a dairy task force.
We are inviting dairy farmers and other participants to engage with the Government in trying to sort out a deal with all these very important issues. I hope I will have the support of the Hon. Member in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister knows that diary farmers are very concerned that the Government has agreed to a deal whereby their prices can go down but their prices and incomes cannot go up until 1991.
The Minister has not indicated in his answer that he is prepared to put in place an indexation mechanism until 1991. Why would the Government agree to a deal
Oral Questions
whereby farmers' incomes can go down but cannot go up until the year 1991?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I just told the Hon. Member, the actions of the Government do not support that proposition. When the cost of the production formula was to trigger a downward price in the target price, the Government of Canada ignored the reality of that and maintained the price level. We still have that same flexibility under the arrangement to which the Hon. Member refers.
I invite the dairy farmers of Canada and others, including the Hon. Member, to participate with us in working out this very important issue, the trade issue, the future of the five-year dairy policy, the cost of production formula, the transferral of quotas, and all those things that have an effect upon the dairy industry in Canada.
We would like to work at it from a constructive basis, not the destructive course that the Hon. Member is on.

subsubtopic: THE NEW SALES TAX-REQUEST AS TO WHETHER MINISTER IN AGREEMENT WITH MINISTER OF CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. I am sure the Minister would agree that his colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, is a man of integrity. On Saturday June 10, when he spoke at a meeting of the Consumers' Association of Canada, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs told a Toronto newspaper that the new sales tax would not be hidden. I quote:

"Visibility, I think, is the only way to ensure that consumers in the end don't get ripped off".

The Minister was right. We know that. Consumers know that. I therefore want to ask the Minister of Finance whether he agrees with his colleague, the

June 21, 1989
Oral Questions
Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, that the only way to ensure that consumers are not ripped off is to make the new sales tax a visible part of the price.

subsubtopic: THE NEW SALES TAX-REQUEST AS TO WHETHER MINISTER IN AGREEMENT WITH MINISTER OF CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me remind my hon. friend of what I stated in a previous answer. When we have an existing sales tax that is buried deep in the production process it results in a spread between the high effective rate and the low effective rate.
Let me again give some examples: household appliances six and a half points; watches, four points. There is no consistency with the existing tax. The effective rate of tax at the retail level may be 3 per cent, 5 per cent, 10 per cent, or 13.5 per cent.
With this new tax it will be quite clear that on all taxable goods and services it will be 9 per cent. We will be moving away from the hidden tax that we have today, the manufactured sales tax, to one that is quite transparent for the consumer to see.

Mr. Speaker, it will still be a hidden tax. It will still be easy to raise that tax without the consumer being aware of it.
Whether it is special charitable tax status for their friends, windfall profits for tobacco companies, or tax deductions for free traders, when it comes to tax breaks the average Canadian gets the short end of the stick with this Government.
Will the Minister defend the interests of average Canadians and withdraw this ill-conceived "now you see it, now you don't" sales tax?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member states that the consumer will not be aware. If there is ever a change in the sales tax, the consumer will be very much aware of that. The rate at the retail level will be the same for all goods and services that are taxable.
The Hon. Member talks about the average Canadian, and do we have an interest in protecting the average Canadian. Yes, and that will be very clear when this technical paper comes out.
In that technical paper the Hon. Member will see that we have enhanced the value of the refundable sales tax
credit for people in the low and lower middle income brackets. We are ensuring the objective that we set out in the Budget of families earning less than $30,000 being better off after this sales tax reform.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member makes a statement that is not factual, that there has been a breach. What there is is a misunderstanding or a misinterpretation. There is a misinterpretation on behalf of one of the parties that negotiated the lease.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
1. Yes, the Department has rectified these problems by rigorously monitoring vessel construction, crew training and professional marine management of vessels. What action, if any, has the Department of Fisheries and Oceans taken to resolve the problems, as outlined in the 1988 Auditor General's Report, that the fish inspection program faces considerable pressures in that the training for inspectors is insufficient, there are inconsistencies in standards and procedures, manuals are often out of date, and that weaknesses in management control exist?
Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and
Oceans): While the Department, through its 1986 reorganization, had taken steps to focus time and energy to ensure inspectors have the best possible training and tools for their work, one should also consider the Auditor General's statement regarding the inspection program in which he stated "we were impressed throughout the audit by the high international reputation of Canada's fish inspection program. Few other countries have such a comprehensive system.
Also noteworthy is the department's work with industry to improve fish product quality." The public can have confidence in the fish inspection system due to its multi-facetted nature involving inspection of vessels, unloading practices, raw product, transportation, plants processing practices, and final product. While the Department is taking, and has taken, action to ensure that the Canadian fish inspection system remains as one of the best in the world, the multi-facetted approach provides assurance that the fish now on the market meets standards in spite of the limitations of any one aspect of the inspection program. Any problems that did exist resulted from a lack of central direction and control. In 1986 the Department undertook a major reorganization that, among other things, centralized authority and accountability for the inspection program. As noted in the report, many initiatives to improve management of the inspection program were being planned or were under development at the time of the audit, but at the time of the audit the improvements had not had an impact at the inspector level. Since the audit, a Fish Products Inspection Manual has been issued to inspectors and results are being felt at the field level.

The following outlines the action taken to date in response to specific comments regarding fish inspection which the Auditor General made in his 1988 Report.
-Sampling. The Auditor General raised concerns regarding the Department's sampling plans. The Department has been evaluating an alternative internationally recognized sampling plan for two years and is now implementing major pilot projects to test the new sampling plan under practical conditions. If the pilot projects prove that the new sampling plan performs as expected, the new plan will be introduced early in 1990.
-Inconsistencies in standards and procedures. The Department issued the "Fish Products Inspection Manual Policies and Procedures" to all inspectors in February of this year. While the "Fish Products Inspection Manual Standards and Methods" is scheduled to be released this year, six (6) specific product standards and methods chapters have already been forwarded to the field for use and other standards and methods will be released shortly. By the end of 1989/90 more than 80 per cent of all fish products will be covered by newly revised standards and methods.
The "Metal Can Defect Manual" will be published this month. The Facilities Inspection Manual will be released as a first draft by July.
These new manuals and standards will complete the task of reissuing a revised set of instructions to all staff.
-Training. The Auditor General raised concerns over training. The Department has been developing national training packages for some time. Inspectors will be evaluated in 1989/90 to determine their specific training needs. Training will be delivered in 37 training modules. Twenty (20) modules are now complete and training will commence in 1989/90. University level courses in sensory evaluation for inspectors started in 1986/87 and are continuing.
-Inspector Testing. Inspector testing continues with respect to tuna. A series of workshops will be held in June to lay the groundwork for testing inspectors evaluations of other products. Work on chemical indicators of spoilage is continuing and will help in the testing of inspectors. A national inspection laboratory was estab-
Order Paper Questions
lished in 1988 in Ottawa and is now equipped and staffed to assist in work on chemical indicators of spoilage.
-Management Weakness. Management weakness in information systems and program control are being addressed through the development of a comprehensive Management Information System (MIS) that will indicate where effort is spent and what results are achieved. Portions of the MIS will be completed in 1989/90 and in conjunction with the work on manuals and audits will provide improved management control.
-Field Reviews. Audits of field application of standards and compliance to policies and procedures will start in early 1990.
-In-Plant Quality Control. The Auditor General questioned why the Department does not use existing company in-plant quality control systems to help assure that standards are met. The Department is now moving ahead with implementation of a comprehensive Quality Management Program that will involve coordinated company and government action to ensure that standards are met.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Tiirner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government has applied closure to the Bill and closed off debate. It has locked out the unemployed of our country and told those without a job in Canada, "We don't have any more time to talk about you". That is the type of hammer that the Government has applied against the unemployed in Canada.
This debate is about how we as a nation treat people who, through no fault of their own, have lost their jobs. This debate is about whether or not we believe that governments at all levels, particularly the Government in Ottawa, have a commitment to help Canadian workers

Unemployment Insurance Act
when they need that help the most, when they become unemployed.
With this legislation the Government is pulling out of the most basic of our social programs, the most fundamental element of the social net of Canada, the unemployment insurance, protecting as it has for more than 40 years the unemployed of this country, as a matter not of discretion but as a matter of right, and as a matter going to the pride of every Canadian worker, and not a matter of welfare. By pulling $2 billion out of the unemployment insurance program, leaving it merely to employers and employees to finance the program, it is privatizing unemployment insurance. It is privatizing the most fundamental social program in this country.
Hear, hear!

It is part of the same agenda through which we have seen privatization everywhere: we suffer the dilution in the privatizing of our transportation infrastructure, selling off Air Canada, the public air transport in the country, closing down rail transportation and passenger service at VIA Rail, closing down the rural post offices and the rural postal routes, abandoning regional economic development, shutting down rural and small-town Canada, and now destroying our social programs by privatizing them and leaving the unemployed to their own resorts.
We now see the Americanization of our national policies in full flight as a result of the trade agreement, as a result of the philosophy of the Speech from the Throne, as a result of the philosophy inherent in the Budget, and now, of course, as a result of this legislation cutting unemployment insurance.
We have known for some time, and we have brought it to the attention of the Government, that the American government has always considered unemployment insurance an unacceptable subsidy offending the meaning of its trade legislation, the 1930 Trade Act, the 1974 Trade Act, and the omnibus trade bill passed by the Congress last year. This Government pulled out of unemployment insurance before the negotiations on the definition of subsidy ever began. It knuckled under once again to the American government. As part of the trade agreement,
it privatized unemployment insurance at the expense of the Canadian worker in favour of American business.
The Tory solution as to how Canada should treat people who lose their jobs, through no fault of their own, is to cut $2 billion out of the unemployment insurance program, to make unemployment insurance more difficult to receive by extending the period needed to qualify for benefits, and by making the benefit period shorter. It is like throwing an anchor out to a drowning man.

This Bill reflects an attitude that considers people who lose their jobs not as powerless victims of economic circumstances but as lazy, good-for-nothing bums who don't deserve our help and support. As was pointed out by the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) on June 6 here in the House, our Party agrees with the need to reduce the deficit but never at the expense of the unemployed, the sick, the disabled, the poor and the destitute.
The Conservative Government does not agree. It believes that the best way to reduce the deficit is to do so at the expense of the weakest and neediest members of our society.
Shame!

That is why it has
decided to reduce unemployment insurance benefits. It is easier to run roughshod over people who can't defend themselves, people without influence, the underclasses, people who are powerless in their own country. The same attitude is reflected in the Government's approach to the new sales tax, in the cuts applied to childcare expenses, the reductions in transfer payments for education and health and the incredible tax increases this Government has imposed on Canadian families since 1984, families on low and middle incomes, while at the same time providing tax relief for the rich.

This Bill is the further implementation of the Tories' right-wing agenda, an agenda they kept hidden and secret during the election campaign. They kept it secret because they knew that the vast majority of Canadians would simply not accept such Draconian and cowardly measures. The Tories did not merely keep silent about that agenda, they did not merely keep silent about their
June 21, 1989

real intentions, they went one step further. They deliberately misled Canadians by saying they would never touch unemployment insurance.
I want to take Members to a scene before a whole host of Conservative supporters at the Hotel Newfoundland in St. John's on October 13. In response to reporters, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) stated: "The federal Government has no plans to make changes to the unemployment insurance program". Those were the words of the Minister for International Trade. Of course, in St. John's the reporters know him well, so they asked him if he had checked this with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). The Prime Minister was in the same room with him speaking to the same gathering of Conservatives. In response to that question from reporters, the Minister stated: "You're damn right I asked him about it and he said no, no one is planning any changes in the unemployment insurance program". That is what was stated by the Minister for International Trade on the authority of the Prime Minister of Canada a few days before the election.
To put it bluntly, either the Prime Minister did not tell the truth to the Minister for International Trade, or the Minister for International Trade did not tell the truth to the Canadian people. I suspect that neither of them told the truth to the Canadian people.
Everyone in the country knows that this legislation will shift people off unemployment insurance and onto welfare. As reported in Hansard on June 6, at page 2677, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) stated: "Nothing could be further from the truth".
How does the Minister of Employment and Immigration respond to the Tory Premier of Nova Scotia, Mr. Buchanan? He had this to say about the changes announced by the Minister: "This is of grave concern to me because that means there is a transfer of funding for these people from the unemployment insurance books to our social service books". The Premier is absolutely correct.
We have asked for the impact studies on which this legislation is based.
Unemployment Insurance Act

In fact, the Government has given no thought at all to the potential impact of these measures on the unemployed, let alone the provincial governments. The changes made within the program will also have the effect of taking money out of the pockets of the unemployed to put it into training programs.
Our Party wants training and skills upgrading programs, and it has demanded those for years. We need more of these programs. However, we always took the position that funds earmarked for training programs would come out of the country's general Budget or be provided jointly by business and the government.
Now today, after cutting training and retraining programs for four and a half years, the Government discovers that training is important. However, instead of creating new ways to finance training programs, the Government takes money from the unemployed to pay for these programs.
What will happen is that poorly paid workers in labour-intensive industries will finance the training of skilled workers who hold highly technical jobs in industries that do not employ many workers.
The new programs, which have not yet been announced, will not apply equally to all regions and are not transferable. An unemployed person in Newfoudland cannot be trained to be an auto worker. People who lose their jobs in regions that offer no other employment opportunities will have their unemployment insurance benefits reduced to pay for training programs in which they cannot take part.
And to justify these brutal changes, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) says that the unemployed do not pay for unemployment insurance, that only those who have a job pay into it, and that therefore, the Government is not taking money from the unemployed.
Of course, the opposite is true: the unemployed will pay for these cuts. They will pay by receiving less money than they would be entitled to under the present program. It is completely wrong to say that the unemployed will not pay.

June 21, 1989
Unemployment Insurance Act

The Minister of State for Employment and Immigration (Mrs. Vezina) told the House last Friday: "We are not cutting our programs, we are making them more effective and more productive".
How does the Minister explain that to an employee of a small trucking company in Moncton where the unemployment rate is now 11.3 per cent? How can she explain that it is "more effective", to use her words, to be required to work four weeks longer to qualify for any unemployment insurance benefits, and that it is not cutting the program when they will be entitled to seven weeks less of insurance payments?
What does the Government say to the clerk in Comer Brook where there is an unemployment rate of 17.6 per cent? How is it more effective for that person to receive three weeks less in unemployment insurance cheques?
How does the Government explain to the miner in Sudbury, where the unemployment rate is 8.5 per cent, that working six more weeks to qualify and then receiving five weeks less in benefits is not cutting benefits?
What does the Government tell the unemployed lumberman in the Kootenays, where the unemployment rate is 12.1 per cent, who will now need three more weeks work to qualify and who will receive eight weeks less in unemployment insurance?
What does the Minister and the Prime Minister suggest unemployed parents tell their children when there is not enough money to put food on the table, or to buy proper clothing, or to find an adequate and decent place to live?
We are seeing here a Government that ascribes to the big lie theory, practised by so many deceitful regimes around the world to justify their actions. The method is simple. If something is said often enough and loud enough it eventually becomes the truth.
Here is what the Prime Minister said during the French television debate with myself and the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent). "We shall maintain all our social programs, without fail. There is nothing in the Free Trade Agreement that will prevent us from fulfilling these obligations, nor in the future, and we intend to spend more on these programs".
Is cutting $2 billion out of unemployment insurance and making people wait longer for fewer benefits how you would describe the way a Government would maintain "all our social programs without fail", Mr. Speaker? Mr. Speaker, would you say that that was how you would "spend more on these programs"? Of course you would not, Mr. Speaker. That is what the Tory Government says. That is what it expects Canadians to believe.
Canadians no longer believe this incessant propaganda of the federal Government. What they are now seeing is the Government's agenda being completely unmasked. The unemployment insurance cuts, the Budget, the trade deal and the Throne Speech make that perfectly clear.
The agenda is clearly laissez-faire, but markets run the countiy. Members of the Government have been following a cynical and calculatedly callous public agenda aimed at cutting everything for the average Canadian to make way for the market forces which will benefit the rich and powerful among us. It has become and is becoming the law of the jungle. It is a world in which only the strongest and richest will survive.
We have said in the House before that there is nothing wrong with business-but the business of business is money and profit, which is fine. The business of public life is people. The mistake this Government is making is that it confuses the two and does not make a distinction between them.
Hear, hear!

I have said before that I believe in market forces and in competition. I believe in rewarding success. I believe in entrepreneur-ism. However, Mr. Speaker, you know and I know that the country would not have been built solely on market forces. We built this country east and west and north by resisting the overwhelming continental market forces of the United States. That is why we built a national railway, a national highway, a public broadcasting system, and a national health care system. That is why we had a national public unemployment insurance system paid for by the people of Canada and contributed to by employers and employees alike.
We did those things because we believe as Canadians that the role of our Parliament and the role of our Government is to defend those who cannot defend themselves. I believe that the vast majority of Cana-
June 21, 1989

dians share this point of view. These values are reflected in programs of fairness that we have built over 122 years.
I am confident that these values can endure. I am confident that Canadians want these values to endure. That is why we will continue to give a voice to those values, to help Canadians understand what is really behind the Tory agenda, what is really behind the philosophy of this Bill, what the Tory Government is doing to make this a very, very different country from the country that we have known.
We have just been present at a vote, the results of which will apply closure against this Bill. Members opposite have the majority. We alone in the Opposition cannot defeat this Bill, which will rob unemployed Canadians of the means to support themselves and their families. Therefore, I want to ask every one of the Conservative back-benchers to consider in his or her conscience just what they are doing here. I want each and every one of the Conservative back-benchers to consider the unemployed in their own riding, the potential unemployed in their ridings and to consider the devastating impact this measure will have on families across the country, in their ridings.
There is no monopoly on unemployment. There is no monopoly on suffering. I want to appeal to the Conservative back-benchers to consider just what they will do at 1 a.m. tomorrow morning in this vote. Each one ought to ask: Is it fair for a federal Government, justified by this Parliament, to make unemployed workers pay the cost of new training programs? I want every one of the Conservative back-benchers to think about whether they really want their constituents pushed off unemployment insurance and onto welfare. I want every Conservative backbencher to acknowledge that there is a fundamental difference between being on unemployment insurance, a right of citizenship, and being on welfare. Anyone who does not know the difference between the two does not know what Canada is all about.
Hear, hear!

A fair and fully funded unemployment insurance program leaves the unemployed with a degree of pride. No fault is attached to the accident of unemployment. No degree of blame
Unemployment Insurance Act
isput on those who, through no fault of their own, find themselves without a job. Compare that with the indignity and shame of having to go to a food bank, or having to line up for welfare, and then people will know what we are talking about on this side of the House.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, you do not solve problems of unemployment by taking money away from the unemployed. We cannot solve the problems of poverty by taking money away from the poor. We cannot solve the Government's problems of the deficit by attacking the people who can least afford to bear that burden. We do not build a better country by tearing down the rights of the disadvantaged.
We have seven hours of debate left on this Bill. I want to ask every Member of Parliament to use every bit of time given to us as freely elected members of the people to bring these issues to the highest court in the land. The greatest privilege any Canadian citizen can have is the one shared by Members of Parliament to represent the weak, the disenfranchised, the disenchanted, those who have not been getting the same opportunities as so many of us have.
I urge every Member of Parliament to join with us at 1 a.m. tomorrow morning, to stand up for the rights and the dignity of Canadian workers, to stand up for the rights of citizenship of a publicly financed unemployment insurance scheme, to stand up for the most fundamental of our social programs, to stand up by voting against this Draconian, repressive, regressive piece of legislation. That is my plea to Members on all sides of the House.
Hear, hear!

speechtext: Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing (Mr. Axwort-hy).

Mr. Speaker, in the five minutes remaining to complete my remarks, I want to continue in the same vein indicating the tragic consequences that will arise as a result of these Draconian measures included in the changes to the unemployment insurance legislation.

June 21, 1989
Unemployment Insurance Act
The people in my riding see the unemployment rate increasing rather than decreasing and it is not satisfactory to them that their benefits under UI are decreasing when there are no job opportunities for them.
Also, the money which may come from the savings the Government will be making by taking funds out of UI are not likely to be introduced into far-sighted programs but rather into the same short-time shortsighted programs that have existed to date.
The proposals do not make it clear exactly how the Government can justify its hope that the private sector, which in the past has done a woefully inadequate job of retraining and educating workers, will take up this retraining torch and do anything other than look after the private sector's own short-term interests.
The Government's figures indicate that some of the
300,000	Canadians who are currently eligible for UI benefits will not be after these changes take effect. Three hundred thousand Canadians will be thrown on the welfare rolls rather than have the opportunity to obtain UI benefits to which they have contributed throughout their working lives. Without access to the impact studies which the Government must surely have conducted, it is difficult to be precise. Even using these figures, the cost to local economies across the country will, of course, be tragic. The Government's action represents in particular a clear attack on the regions, including the interior of B.C., rural Alberta, the Atlantic Provinces, the North, northern Ontario, north and eastern Quebec and, of course, Saskatchewan. All these areas of the country will suffer an inexcusable and vicious attack.
To compound the problem the federal Government is also banning its support for regionally extended benefits and in so doing is denying any responsibility for regional differences in employment rates which frequently are a direct result of failed federal Government policies. At the present time we are also finding increasingly that federal Government policies are attacking the regions rather than assisting them. This one-two punch is completed when we consider that the Minister of Finance's Budget cuts large amounts of funding destined for many one-industry towns. Entire regions are placed in jeopardy by the Government that sees only balance sheets and accounting formula rather than people.
It is clear that the Bill is a product of the Government's neo-Conservative philosophy rather than any thoughtful government planning.
There are some areas of this legislation which are positive. For example, recognition of the rights of natural parents under the unemployment insurance system is a positive step. But the Government can hardly be said to be visionaiy on this matter. So too are improvements to sickness benefits which now enable individuals to file for benefits regardless of when, during their claim, they become ill. Another positive step is the change to benefit access afforded to Canadians over 65 years of age.
Once again the Government fought this every step of the way and only after court decisions against the Government did it move to correct these problems.
On behalf of my caucus colleagues and all those across the country who fought long and hard to convince the Government that injustices were being done under the UI system, I think we owe our deepest congratulations for their efforts which have helped move this Government a few steps closer to understanding the need for legislation which is both sensible and sensitive.
I want to conclude by saying that this Bill is more about dividing and conquering than it is about improving the unemployment insurance system. Time after time and clause after clause this Government pits region against region, worker against worker, for an ever shrinking number of dollars.
I do not recall the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) travelling around the country during the election telling people: " Vote for me and I will cut your UI benefits. Vote for me and I will cancel the child care plan. Vote for me and I will cut the amount of money you get through EPF. Vote for me and I will harmonize our nation's social programs with those in the United States. Vote for me and I will make the biggest tax grab in Canadian history".
I do not remember him saying those things, but in the end that surely is what he should have said if he was going to be straightforward and honest with the Canadian people.
These are some of the first shots in the harmonization battle, a battle, I am sad to say, my Party predicted would take place. I will predict that in the weeks and months ahead other similar pieces of legislation will be placed before this House and, as with Bill C-21, the New Democrats will stand firm in their opposition to this kind of regressive legislation. In closing, the Government
June 21, 1989

must start to put people first. For example, the over 12 per cent unemployed in Saskatoon want jobs, not cuts to UI benefits of $1.3 billion a year.
