reconnaissance, no airborne environmental and drug surveillance and a delay in the response of search and rescue operations. In addition, the Government has so mismanaged the fishery in Atlantic Canada that fish plant after fish plant has closed while foreign overfishing continues and even, it seems, is being encouraged to continue.
To top everything the Government, after hacking its way through every economic sector including tourism, and creating even higher levels of unemployment throughout Atlantic Canada, is now going to make it more difficult to qualify for unemployment insurance. This is an example of the new government mathematics. It states that less plus less equals more. The Government is going to cut $2.9 billion out of the unemployment commission moneys.
I would like to take a few minutes now to show how the new unemployment insurance changes will affect Prince Edward Island. First, the new changes will have a negative impact calculated by the Government to be 10.3 per cent. This can be compared to our sister Atlantic provinces where the negative impact will be only 4.6 per cent and to Canada as a whole where the negative impact will be 5.2 per cent. These are the Government's own figures. As you see, Mr. Speaker, Prince Edward Island will suffer twice the negative impact of the country as a whole and twice the negative impact of the other Atlantic provinces, and the Government calls this fair and equitable treatment.
I have three questions I want to address concerning unemployment insurance. They are, one, what role does UI play in the provincial economy of Prince Edward Island; two, what impact will the proposed UI changes have on Prince Edward Island; and three, what is position of P.E.I. on the proposed changes?
Today unemployment insurance is one of the most important programs in Atlantic Canada, and it is especially so in Prince Edward Island. In fact, in 1988, Prince Edward Islanders received more than $138 million in benefits, or $1,076 for every man, woman and child in the Province compared to $422 for Canada as a whole. Further, the UI program provides more money to the provincial economy than some of the industries in the province. For example, last year an average of 11,000 persons received UI benefits in P.E.I. out of an average labour force of 62,000, which is 18 per cent. In other words, approximately one out of five Islanders in the

Unemployment Insurance Act
labour force relied on UI benefits at some time during the year. This is due primarily to our seasonal economy.
Clearly the direct impact of this program is very far-reaching. There are also significant indirect impacts. Islanders spent their UI benefits as consumers which, in turn, creates spin-off employment and thus impacts, not only on those who receive benefits, but also on the retail trade and on the service sectors. That is why UI plays such a vital role in a seasonal resource-based economy such as P.E.I.
Allow me at this time, Mr. Speaker, to describe the economy of P.E.I. to you. There are 128,000 people living on Prince Edward Island, and natural resources are the backbone of our economy. We are blessed with good, arable land, so agriculture is one of our major industries. We are an island so we have access to fish stocks such as lobster, cod, scallops, herring, oysters and so on. The beauty of our island is another natural resource, one that attracts more than 700,000 visitors each year. These are our basic industries; land, fish, and natural beauty. The industries which utilize these resources are, by their very nature, seasonal. There are, of course, other industries in P.E.I., but a significant percentage of our labour force is dependent on these seasonal industries.
The UI program supports the needs of those employed in seasonal jobs while at the same time supporting the needs of private sector employers in the rural areas of our country.
Why is UI so important? It is because you cannot fish lobster or process fish during the winter. We have a slight problem with ice around Prince Edward Island during the winter. It is because potatoes cannot be grown during the winter and it is because our tourist resort areas become like ghost towns during the winter. That is why we require UI, in order to supplement the incomes of those Islanders who cannot find work as well as those who cannot find full-time work.
The proposal to increase the number of weeks worked to qualify for UI benefits is based on the erroneous assumption that there are more weeks of employment available and that people just do not want to work them.
P.E.I. has a very short tourist season. July and August are the high season tourist months with a shorter season in June and September. What are Islanders supposed to do to get the number of required weeks if their employer only operates 10 weeks a year? Does the federal Government expect those employers to stay open longer when there are no tourists and there is no income? We cannot ask our tourists to ignore the fact that they cannot swim in May or October. We cannot ask our potato farmers to harvest their crop in December. Our economy is a seasonal one.
The role UI plays in our provincial economy is one of tremendous importance. The proposed changes will significantly impact on Islanders who can least afford it. The question is, what is the real impact of the proposed UI changes? The impact can be described in one word, "devastating". We know that our province will be the one most affected by the proposed changes.
We have, with the data available, calculated some of the repercussions for P.E.I. Given the increase in the number of work weeks required to draw UI benefits, P.E.I. could lose as much as $18 million. A reduction in the length of benefits could mean a loss of another $6 million. The impact on provincial government programs such as welfare assistance has not been included in these estimates but they will add to the increase. In total, based on a conservative estimate, and I do not use that word in a pejorative sense here, P.E.I. could lose as much as $27 million in UI benefits alone which would result in very significant spin-off losses as well.
One of the arguments made in defence of the changes is that P.E.I. will lose benefits but gain additional dollars through the Labour Force Development Strategy. In order for this argument to apply, the federal Government would have to do two things; first, it would have to institute an extensive and comprehensive job creation program. There is no point in training people for jobs which do not exist unless they want to force people to move to central Canada. Second, it would have to negotiate extensively with provinces to ensure that the programs are responsive to the uniqueness of each region in this country.

The diversity of this country must be recognized in the Labour Force Development Strategy. The new strategy should not be solely driven by private sector training. The whole thrust of the Canadian Jobs Strategy is to involve the private sector in providing training. P.E.I. has a very small private sector, one which can only do so much training. How many times can you ask the same employer to train the unemployed for jobs that do not exist? It is not feasible to expect the limited private sector in our province to provide more meaningful and effective training for the unemployed, especially if they have to absorb a significant portion of the cost.
The federal proposal to change UI will substantially reduce benefits to Islanders but the program proposed to replace them will not substantially benefit Islanders unless the programs are sensitive to the provincial economy. The training programs must be geared towards a growth that will provide long-term jobs with a large number of private sector employers. Unfortunately that does not describe the current economy of P.E.I.
The final question to be addressed is the position of P.E.I. on the proposed UI changes. P.E.I. has a unique economy. The current UI program recognizes and complements that uniqueness. This country is made up of diverse regions. Indeed the success of the country is based on recognizing the strengths and weaknesses of each region. We rely on UI in our region. We sincerely wish that we did not have to do that. All provinces, especially P.E.I., would like to have a booming economy that creates full-time jobs. However, the reality is that we do not. Programs must recognize and deal with the reality of each province. Each province is unique in its own right. In fact, Canada is diversity. Therefore, all programs must be both receptive and responsive to the needs of all Canadians. The current UI program has been successful in respecting that criteria.
This is not to suggest that there are not some positive proposals in the Labour Force Development Strategy. The Maternal Parental Sickness Benefits Program will in fact benefit Canadians. The proposed arrangements will provide more generous income protection for those Canadians involved. Furthermore, providing benefits to those over the age of 65 corrects an inequity which existed within the UI system.
Unemployment Insurance Act
Permitting workers on sickness or maternity benefits during a labour dispute to receive benefits also eliminates an unfair situation for those workers. While there is some merit in some of the proposed UI changes, however, I must say clearly and unequivocably, P.E.I. does not support increasing the number of weeks required to draw benefits and decreasing the number of weeks those benefits can be collected.
There is another aspect of the Government's proposed UI program with which I strongly disagree, and that is the Government's decision to withdraw from the funding of the program. It would seem that the federal Government has a responsibility to Canadians from Vancouver to St. John's, Newfoundland. We cannot shirk that responsibility by suggesting that employers and employees should absorb the total cost of a program designed and administered by the federal Government.
I would also like to address another critical issue in our province, and that is the announcement in the federal Budget of the closure of the Canadian Forces Base at Summerside. Closure of this base would have a tremendous effect on Prince Edward Island and on the Summerside economy.
There are more than 1,300 direct jobs at stake, as well as 2,000 indirect jobs. This represents 4.4 per cent of employment in the province. Our unemployment rate could increase to 60 per cent or higher. This would be a most devastating blow to our province. If Ontario or Quebec were to lose the same percentage of jobs, it would represent over 200,000 jobs in those two provinces.
There would not be enough ink in the newspapers in Upper and Lower Canada to tell the people of the country how devastating this would be, and how they would force the Government to change its mind if any government was going to take 200,000 jobs out of the economy of Toronto or Montreal.
How would a federal Member from Ontario feel if that number of jobs were lost? How would their Premier feel?
People in Prince Edward Island are for just and equitable treatment. I urge this Government to reconsider its decision. Our economy cannot absorb such a tremendous increase in the number of unemployed. The

June 21, 1989
Unemployment Insurance Act
closure of CFB Summerside will further increase regional disparity. We will become more and more the poor cousins of Canada.
My request is simple and clear. Change the decision. Do not increase the number of weeks required to draw unemployment insurance. Do not reduce the number of weeks of benefits which can be drawn.
P.E.I. cannot accept closure of Canadian Forces Base in Summerside. Our economy in Prince County depends on the base for its survival. It contributes more to the economy of Prince County than the fishery. Our feelings run so deep on this issue that doubt is now being cast by our Premier on his support for the Meech Lake Accord.
In conclusion, Canada is a great country. We are admired throughout the world for our ability to respect diversity. We respect the uniqueness of our provinces. This principle forms a foundation of our country. Programs such as UI and defence spending respect that principle. Changing the number of weeks required to draw, and reducing the duration of benefits, as well as the closing of CFB Summerside violates that principle. We must not let that happen. The Government is sowing the wind, and they will reap the whirlwind.

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):

speechtext:

People watch to see what happens afterward. They look for a scorched earth policy and they find that after all it is not a scorched earth policy. Then they do a little bit of a double-take. They say: "Look, we heard this man say it".
I commend him for thinking of the variable needs of Canada, the regions. He said, and I think I quote him accurately, "the policy ought to reflect the regions of
Canada". This is exactly what unemployment insurance does. It reflects the needs of the regions of Canada. There are variable unemployment rates across Canada. The Bill recognizes those various needs across Canada. The Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) was a Member of the Government when that whole concept was brought in. I am sure he voted for it, as a good Member of the Government at the time.
The whole idea of variable entry programs was brought in 10 or 12 years ago, based upon the varying needs of the regions of Canada and the employment needs of those regions. I would encourage the Member for Egmont to keep that in mind as he speaks.
I would point out to him at the same time that if he wants to do that, he should also listen to the party line as espoused by his party leaders on the subject, because his finance critic just three months ago tomorrow, to be exact-
What time?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
were largely blue collar workers. They were usually unorganized and usually had no union leadership.
In the ensuing years, labour has become organized, thankfully. Not only do the labour unions work largely for the blue collar workers, but they also have trained economists on their staff, economists with M.BAs and so forth. The conditions have changed.
We have tripartite agreements and arrangements. Conditions have changed, maybe not the way we want them yet, but the circumstances are different. The unemployment insurance Bill is designed to be flexible enough to meet the changing conditions in Canada.
I ask Members to read a book like "Mega Trends", which was published a few years ago, and is simply a composite of magazine and newspaper articles. They are statements from opinion makers from around the world outlining what the mega trends are for the world, and therefore, for each of the economies in the world.
By and large, the message of that book is that the labour force, particularly in the western world but certainly in the other countries too, is changing. Conditions are changing. We have moved from an industrial society in the western world to an information society. There are entirely different kinds of working conditions. There are entirely different kinds of labour contracts.
Unemployment is still the same.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Unemployment hurts just as much as it ever did before. It sure does. That is why we need the protection that unemployment insurance gives. Unemployment insurance is not the insurance people need the most. They need the opportunity to get a job. We need changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act to enable workers to change to the circumstances that exist in our society.
I know that my conservative friends in the NDP want nothing to change because they are the most conservative people in this House. They want nothing to change. If something is entrenched, keep it that way, because we
Unemployment Insurance Act
might lose something. There is no risk involved in that Party. The NDP do not want risk at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada

What we want to do is use that money in such a way that people can adjust to changing circumstances. The Members opposite think circumstances never change. They want things to stay as they always have. When you are in a leadership role, as this Government is, people recognize that circumstances change. We have technological change here in Canada. The sooner Members of the Opposition wake up to that, the better off they will be. They will start representing the workers as soon as they recognize that.
The Bill introduces a labour force development strategy. Workers who are unemployed can retrain themselves, use their talents and apply them in a new way in the workplace and get the jobs they want. Not only do workers have to adjust, but so do employers. Opposition Members may want to heckle me on some points but I think they will agree with me that in Canada employers need to get behind the whole concept of training and retraining employees. Canada lags behind the industrial countries in this case. It certainly lags behind the United States. It is time for our industrial leaders to think in
terms of their employees and adapting them to changing circumstances.
The private sector now has to assume a leadership role in the training of workers as it has done in other industrialized nations. We have to do this in Canada. In some cases it will help them to relocate to places where there are better job prospects.

I note that you say my time is up, Mr. Speaker. I know that will disappoint Members opposite. I want to assure them that Canadians who deserve support have support under this legislation. It exists and will continue to exist. The unemployed of Canada can count on it, and I know

they will count on the kind of support this program gives to them.

Mr. Speaker, we just heard from the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) a glib, shallow and incoherent intervention. He supports this Bill because it is change for the sake of change. He is asking the unemployed of his riding to read the speeches of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulro-ney) to find comfort when they are unemployed and run out of benefits. He is an embarrassment to his own Party and to this own colleagues, coming as he does from an area of high unemployment.
Earlier, I was surprised by the intervention of the Hon. Member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley) who spoke with his fat cat view of the world. The Hon. Member for Don Valley West and the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock, I am sure, share the same basic philosophy. They believe in the market-place, and the Hon. Member for Don Valley West made a speech underlining the importance of the market-place.
When it comes to the unemployed, when it comes to the little people, when it comes to those who cannot defend themselves in the market-place, he believes in the importance of the market-place. However, when it comes to large corporations, when it comes to giving subsidies to large oil and gas companies, when it comes to giving support to megaprojects, all of a sudden there is a conversion; then he believes in subsidies and he no longer believes in the market-place.
How can one be consistent, convincing and politically in line with the thinking of Canadians with such a contradiction in terms? How can one be convincing in the eyes of one's constituents by speaking such profound, basic nonsense? The market-place has to work for the little people but, my gosh, they believe in subsidies when it comes to the corporate world.
The Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock and the Hon. Member for Don Valley West will draw unemployment insurance after the next election. They will get a taste of it when their turn will come. I am sure that the former Member for Prince Albert, Mr. Diefenbaker, will be turning in his grave with rage if he heard the speeches made by those two Progressive Conservative Members. He was the great defender of the small people, of the
weak in society. He would turn in his grave if he heard that kind of nonsense.
What is Bill C-21 all about? It is not a question of the deficit. That is a smoke-screen. It is not a question of believing, as we have been accused of, in throwing money to the unemployed in order to solve the question of unemployment. It seems to me that the issue is the integrity of a key social program which has served Canada very well over the last 50 years.
Why do we on this side say that? We are the architects of that social program. It is our product. We made it better over the years. We see the program as being intended as a bridge for people who are between jobs, people who have no control over the vagaries of the market-place, that great market-place in which the Hon. Member for Don Valley West believes so strongly. People do not have control of that and therefore can lose employment and do not know when they will find other employment.
Second, we believe that the program stabilizes the population and provides stability. It prevents Canadians from moving and eventually living in 10 or 11 urban centres. Therefore, it is a very important social role.
Third, it reduces the burden on the provincial treasurers because it takes on responsibility for the unemployed rather than saying as does the Bill: "You take over this burden. Once you run out of your time, you go to the provincial social and family services and ask them to help you".
Fourth, we believe that it facilitates labour market requirements. It would take a lengthy intervention to go into details, but it is obvious that a good unemployment insurance scheme provides for a number of services and economic aids at the moment when needed for people who move from industry to industry, or sometimes even from region to region. We believe it is better to bring the jobs to the people than have the people move to the jobs.
Finally, it provides economic shock absorbers to certain segments in the workforce. For instance, the older workers on which my colleague the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) spoke so eloquently last night. It is a very important economic shock absorber for the older worker. Therefore, we would want to ensure that an older worker who becomes unemployed is not forced to turn to public assistance unduly



June 21, 1989

and too soon, but rather has the dignity of economic support through unemployment insurance until his or her employment situation is hopefully resolved.
Those are the five central pillars of ideology that have so far driven us in the evolution and the development of the unemployment insurance system, in which we believe profoundly. This is why we are here fighting against this measure of closure and the spirit of the Bill itself.

Mr. Speaker, I read with great interest a folder prepared in cooperation with the Regroupement de chomeurs et chomeuses du Quebec entitled Solidarite populaire Quebec and sub-titled, "Unemployment Insurance: $1.3 billion less, 200,000 beneficiaries cut!"
I found some examples on page 3. There is an example that I would like to bring to your attention because it is so typical, it is so well prepared, it describes a kind of working woman that can be found throughout Canada.
It says:
After working for 25 years without interruption in a Montreal candy factory, Christine, 55 years old, earns $333 gross a week. She is no longer able to meet the increased rate of production that her boss requires.
That is very important!
She quits her job. The Commission rules that she does not have a valid reason for quitting her job.
Now, under the present plan, Christine can receive a 6-week penalty and after 6 weeks, 44 weeks of benefits at the normal rate of 60 per cent of her salary.
But after the change with the coming into force of Bill C-21, Christine will have a 12-week penalty and during that time, Christine will not even be entitled to welfare; then she will have 37 weeks of benefits at a reduced rate of 50 per cent of her salary.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if that is social progress, if that is what the Conservative Party which calls itself Progressive has in mind for the Canadian people? I ask you that, Mr. Speaker!
Unemployment Insurance Act

At this point I would like to draw attention, very slowly, but it is necessary, to what will happen to people who become unemployed from British Columbia to Atlantic Canada, for the benefit of those back-benchers of the Tory Party who do not seem to know what will happen when this legislation comes into effect, judging from the speeches that have been made, some of their interventions, and some of their questions.
Starting with British Columbia, in the Kootenays under the present system a worker who becomes unemployed could receive benefits for 42 weeks. When Bill C-21 comes into effect, it will become 34 weeks. In the Kelowna region, the drop will be from 42 weeks at the present time to 33 weeks; in Kamloops from 42 weeks to 37 weeks.
To those Members who come from the Prairies, it is interesting to note that in southern Manitoba under the present system the unemployed worker receives 26 weeks of benefits, and that will drop to 21 weeks. In southern Saskatchewan it will drop from 26 weeks to 21 weeks. In Yorkton and Prince Albert it will drop from 32 weeks to 27 weeks. In the northern part of the prairie provinces it will drop from 42 weeks to 34 weeks.
What is it for Davenport?

In the Liberal Party, we tend to embrace the whole country. We care for the unemployed no matter where they are. An unemployed person in the Yukon is as of much importance to us as if that person were in our own riding. We are responsible to everybody. That is our mandate.
In the remainder of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta the drop is 8 weeks, from 42 weeks to 34 weeks. In eastern Ontario the drop is from 22 weeks to 17 weeks, that is one month and one week less. In Belleville and Peterborough the drop is from 28 weeks to 21 weeks. In Sudbury it is from 29 weeks to 24 weeks; northwestern Ontario, from 28 weeks to 21 weeks; Windsor, from 22 weeks to 17 weeks; and Sarnia, from 25 weeks to 19 weeks.
This is where the unemployment is. This is where we have to concentrate our attention. These people do not

June 21, 1989
Unemployment Insurance Act
have control of the economy of their own region. When they become unemployed they cannot go off to the next employer across the street, because there are not that many employers.
Let us deal with Quebec.

-in Trois-Rivieres, it will go from 40 weeks now to 33; in the Eastern Townships, from 28 to 24; in the Gaspe, from 42 to 36; in northern Quebec, from 42 to 34-

There are also some pretty drastic drops in Newfoundland. In the Avalon Peninsula the drop is from 42 weeks to 33 weeks. I ask myself, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure you do the same: How can the unemployed men and women in Avalon seek alternative employment in that part of the world?
This is where the greatness of the system comes into play. It provides economic stability and economic insurance, unless one wants to go to Toronto. Perhaps the plan of the Progressive Conservative Government is that all Canadians should live in 11 or 12 cities.
In Prince Edward Island it goes from 42 weeks to 33 weeks. In Halifax it is from 28 weeks to 21 weeks. I am selectively reading, Mr. Speaker. If I were to read every line my time would be gone, and you would not want to miss the rest of my speech.
In Saint John, New Brunswick it goes from 38 weeks to 30 weeks; in Fredericton, from 36 weeks to 30; Madawas-ka-Restigouche, from 42 weeks to 36 weeks. This is a sketch across the nation of what this measure will do.
I wonder what are the feelings and what goes through the minds of Members such as the Members from Abitibi, Mercier, Annapolis Valley-Hants, South Shore, Temiscamingue, Kamouraska-Riviere-du-Loup, Manicouagan, the Gaspe, Pontiac, Peace River, Red Deer, Charlesbourg, Levis, Richmond-Wolfe, Trois-Rivieres, Cumberland-Colchester, Timiskaming, Matapedia-Matane, Beauce, and Bonaventure.
Dispense.

Yes, it hurts. You would like to have it dispensed with.
What goes through the minds of the Members from Brome-Missisquoi, Fundy-Royal, Jonquiere, Chicoutimi, Parry Sound-Muskoka, Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assiniboia, and Crowfoot, just to mention a few Tory ridings? They have not been very vocal in this debate. Actually, they have been strangely silent. I wonder why. Perhaps I am naive.
Perhaps Bill C-21 does not leave much to write home about. That is why they have not been so vocal in this debate. That is why this Bill is coming to a vote tonight in a hurry, fast, because we would not want to have trouble in the back benches of the Progressive Conservative Party. We want to prevent that. When the penny finally drops, when they finally catch up with what is written in Bill C-21, then perhaps they will wake up. However, then it will be tomorrow. It will be too late. That is why there has been such silence.
While the defence budget under the Tories is going up this year, and while subsidies to fossil fuel megaprojects are going up and being maintained to the tune of billions of dollars as a policy of the Government, the Progressive Conservative Government attacks the little people. That is the bottom line of this Bill. In the process it is making a sham of a fine key social program which has served several generations of Canadians so well.
My colleague from Egmont who spoke earlier reminded us that there is not only that but that the Tories have decided also that there is no room for the public sector any longer in the unemployment insurance program. When this Bill comes into effect the Government of Canada will drop its participation in this fund. That is really a sham, a disgrace. It is backward.
The country has been served very well by tripartite forms of government. Unemployment insurance has made progress over the decades because the Government, on behalf of the public, has participated in it with business and labour. Only the Government can speak for those who are not organized. Only the Government can speak for those who are not in business. Thus the tripartite formula is a good one. However, now it will be closed down. This is the end of it. It will be run by two parties-labour and business.
Guess who will run it eventually? I will leave it to you, Mr. Speaker, to guess and to tell us who in the end will run the unemployment insurance program. It does not take a genius to imagine who will do that once it is left to business. Therefore the future of this scheme is doomed

to become weaker and weaker. It will not serve the little people who need it and use it and who have so far benefited from it.
I will conclude on this remark. It is quite revealing that a Conservative Premier in the country-not a Liberal but a Conservative from Nova Scotia-was quoted as saying on Bill C-21: "This is of grave concern to me because that means there is a transfer of funding for these people from the unemployment insurance books to our social service books". Those are the words of Mr. Buchanan, not a wide-eyed radical. This was not a Liberal Premier but a Tory Premier in the Province of Nova Scotia. That is the most severe indictment of this measure that could ever be expected.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity in tonight's debate to address some of the issues before us. I must say that I really was not looking to speak in this particular debate on unemployment insurance, but I am prompted by some of the remarks of Members of the opposition Parties, including the one who just spoke, to do so.
I think their remarks really demonstrate how they are caught in the trap of being prisoners of their own rhetoric. They are hostages of the past. They refuse to learn from the mistakes that they have made and fail to recognize the changes that have been taking place in the labour force in Canada.
I would first like to mention a couple of things prompted by the speech we just heard a moment ago by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). He said that the Government was maintaining support for energy projects while refusing support for unemployment insurance. I will take the remark as it was stated without debating it, for a moment. We see the viewpoint of someone who for some reason or another would prefer to have people receive unemployment insurance than work in a productive capacity.
I know he has concerns about energy megaprojects and some of the environmental considerations connected thereto. However, I want to tell him that while I recognize those concerns I would certainly have to think
Unemployment Insurance Act
that supporting projects that employ people in a positive way, a way in which they can contribute to the economy, has to be of more value than simply paying them not to work. That is what the reforms of this program are all about.
I also want to take a bit of a look at the past because he raised these issues in this way and mention at the start just a few of the things that that former Government did. I am not sure if he was a part of it then, but a look at history is always important.
The unemployment insurance program was created in 1940. One would think that any program created by government from time to time should be reviewed to see whether or not it is meeting the current conditions. In 1971 there was such a review. It was conducted by the Government under the Prime Minister of the day, Mr. Trudeau. His Government overhauled it. When it was changed the most noticeable change we could see was that the costs were doubled. It went from a cost of $900 million per year to $1.8 billion one year later in spite of favourable economic conditions. Presumably, then, this was not something that one would have desired, that is to say, not necessarily the question of the cost but the fact that more people were seeking unemployment insurance. It was becoming something which was seen as an opportunity for income as opposed to working and seeking productive employment.
In 1974 the Liberals decided to make some amendments. I think the changes they made then demonstrate the hypocrisy of what we heard just a moment ago. After being re-elected in 1974 the Liberals decided it was time for belt tightening and introduced three major Bills to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act. The purpose of these measures was one only-to save money.
Bill C-79, which was introduced at that time, took away the right of workers 65 and older to participate in the unemployment insurance program. It reduced the special benefit payment for claimants with dependants, the Bill before us today we are returning the right to persons over 65 years of age to participate in the unemployment insurance scheme. We are reversing a change that was made in 1974 by the government of the day, supported by the Party of the Member who just

Unemployment Insurance Act
spoke, which took away the right of workers over 65 to participate in the system, as a cost-saving measure.
Bill C-27 increased the number of weeks of work needed to collect benefits from eight to between ten and fourteen, depending on the region. It was obviously recognized that there were differences in the regions of this country and therefore a change was made to save money, but done in a way that it affected the regions differently.
Finally, Bill C-14 reduced the maximum amount of benefits from 66.6 per cent to 60 per cent of wages earned, and penalized repeaters who were mostly seasonal workers.
When we lookback at those facts, it is difficult to listen to some of the rhetoric we heard a moment ago with any seriousness at all. Either they have had a mass transformation or they simply adopted what has become the habit of defending everything, to refuse any change, refuse to seek any change and propose no solution.
I want to return to why I believe this Bill should be supported. We do not necessarily gain by looking back 15 years. Rather, we want to look to the future and decide whether what we are trying to do is consistent with society of today and the society we expect in the future.
This Bill is worth supporting primarily for two reasons. First, it is an important step in making the unemployment insurance system responsive and efficient. I believe the changes make it a better program for all of the country, because it gives recognition to the changing nature of our economy.
As Members know, the proposed amendments and the proposed Labour Force Development Strategy are designed to address skills training and employment. The Unemployment Insurance Act amendments are a part of a series of changes in an attempt to make our employment programming more effective. By including the private educational sector and individual employees, the federal Government is making a concerted effort to change the direction of unemployment insurance from an attitude of the Government looking after one's interest to an attitude whereby the Government and industry will help you to get on your feet again soon.
The Government is not doing it any more. They are paying for it themselves.

The Member says the Government is not doing it any more because they are paying for it themselves. We heard earlier from a Member of the New Democratic Party who suggested that because the Government was restructuring the way the program would be financed-
After January, 1990 funding will come out of the workers' pockets.
It was restructured in the way the program would be financed and it will be financed essentially from the premiums. There will not be contributions from the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
That is right.

The Member states that, and it is true. What that seems to imply is that somehow those contributions were coming from somewhere else. It is a game typical of Members in that Party who somehow think we can have more and more and nobody has to pay. They think there is someone else who is paying the bill. The fact is that the unemployment insurance program is either going to be funded by premiums or by income tax or some other tax. If it is funded by income tax, whether the pay cheque deduction at the end of the month is on the line marked unemployment insurance, or the line called Canada Pension Plan, or the line that says income, the person receiving the cheque-
Unemployment insurance is for income support, not for training.

For the person receiving the pay cheque, it does not really make a great difference whether the deduction comes under the fine print of unemployment insurance, CPP or income tax. I suggest that it does not make a difference.
You have never been unemployed, then. I guess you have never been unemployed.
We are not talking about the unemployed.
That is precisely who we are talking about.

The people who are paying for the program are not the unemployed. The unemployed are receiving the benefit. The people who are paying for the program
June 21, 1989

are the employed, the people who are working, earning wages, paying taxes and paying UI premiums.
We can talk all we want, the fact is that a change to paying it from the premiums rather than it simply being taken from the income tax that is deducted from the cheque will give employees an opportunity to see what the program is costing them. It may help them decide whether the program is giving them the value for their money.
I cannot believe that some people would suggest that the money comes from somewhere else. It comes from the same people. There is only one group of taxpayers in this country, and they are either going to pay it in one form or another. I reject the suggestion that changing the system so that premiums will pay the cost of the program will have an adverse impact upon it. The alternative would be to raise income tax or some other tax that Canadians will have to pay in any event.
Maybe corporate tax. How would that be?

The corporate tax is being raised because the corporate premium is being raised. If you want to talk about getting it from the corporations, the corporations will be paying it through the premiums.
It is a sharing of cost by the corporate sector and the employees for a benefit to be paid to people who find themselves out of work for one reason or another.
Let me return to the question of education and training. While we all recognize that in Canada there is a significantly well trained labour force, probably the second best trained labour force in the world, we also realize that other countries are increasing their skill levels, increasing their productivity and their competitiveness. It is important for us to respond.
One way to respond is to give people whose skills may no longer apply to today's market an opportunity to become productive again. Surely, using the unemployment insurance program to do that, rather than simply giving them funds to look for jobs that no longer exist, has to be a step in the right direction.
The day after the Labour Force Development Strategy was discussed on national television, I was contacted by an institution in Edmonton. They were ready to start training more workers immediately, if the Government was willing to help. I know they are hoping for a sound
Unemployment Insurance Act
outcome to this debate and the consultations this summer.
The reason for my support of this Bill is based on a simple premise. That is, Canadians want to work. I am convinced that if we offer them the training and upgrading or the financing to go to work, they will take it.
What about jobs?

For jobs that will be available in new ways because we know that the world is changing. The Member can talk about trying to keep people employed in jobs that no longer exist.
I grew up in a small town. Every small town had a railway station, a bakery, a butcher shop, livery stable and a whole range of businesses that no longer exist today. We will never go back to those days. We will not be able to remain where we are. People have jobs today, jobs that will not exist one year, five years or ten years from now. Those jobs will no longer exist. We cannot try to maintain those jobs in a changing world and the man for the products and services they produce is no longer there. What we have to try to do is to find new jobs for those people and ensure that they are adequately trained to fill them. Five million Canadians a year change jobs. So job change is not the issue. Neither is trying to hold onto jobs that are no longer relevant to today's society. Surely what we want to do is train people for the society of the future.
I want to make a few comments about the capitalization and lump sum payments and how they reflect a commitment to change. Really these are an important statement for individual entrepreneurship. There can really be only three classes where workers go on unemployment insurance. Either they are unemployed for reasons beyond their control, they are temporarily out of the workforce for family reasons, or they have chosen not to work.
In the first scenario, when the person is unemployed for reasons of technology or economics, the proposed changes are improvements. Currently the rationale of the UI program is simply that you will continue to receive benefits until you find another job for which you are qualified, or until you go on another form of social assistance. This is not an exceptionally efficient use of finances, as I said earlier. It is a waste of the workers' time and talents, especially since they may be in a situation where there is really no hope of finding the

Unemployment Insurance Act
kind of jobs that they have been doing in the past. By encouraging the person to get additional education or start a new business venture, we are making an unemployed worker into a better and more productive one.
The second scenario, where employees leave for family reasons, is also being improved with these amendments. Expanded maternity leave and a recognition that adoptive parents as well need time to adjust to the additional person in their lives will make for a more responsive program. With women an increasingly important part of the workforce, these revisions help ensure fairness in the system. The same holds true for older workers who do not want to retire at age 65. By extending benefits, the Government is making the system fairer for those older workers who want to continue in the workforce. That is an important measure because while in the past 20 years we have seen high levels of unemployment, these are in large measure the result of the baby boom after the Second World War with those people coming into the workforce.
In the next 10, 15, 20 years the reverse is going to be true. As these people grow older and begin to reach retirement age, we do not have the numbers coming into the workforce. Therefore, while the problem of the 1970s and the 1980s was one of high unemployment, the problem of the 1990s and the years beyond, in my view, is going to be one of shortage of skilled workers. Therefore, I think it is quite appropriate that whereas in the past we were encouraging people aged 65 or even younger to retire from the workforce, for those who wish to continue we should we give them every opportunity to do so.
I would like to make mention of the people in the third category, those people who choose not to work. There is also a group of amendments and increased penalties for those who abuse the UI system. These are also an integral part of an efficient and fair approach. They make it clear that the UI system is for workers and not for conscientious objectors in the workforce.
I want to talk about fairness in the program. I have a great many constituents who come to see me with various complaints. These amendments move to solve some of the problems, but unfortunately not all of them. For example, I suppose that under the current system,
like the old one, it will still probably take several weeks for the contributor to receive the benefits to which he or she is legitimately entitled. That it can take months to receive a cheque strikes most of my constituents as unfair, especially since they are often receiving benefits for which perhaps they have paid over many months or years in the past. I have also heard from workers who could not collect benefits, and I am pleased to see that that issue is being addressed. I have also heard from people in the taxi industry and in the Armed Forces who currently do not believe the system is fair because they pay premiums and do not receive benefits. At some future time I would like to see that addressed.
On a positive note, the current amendments include a series of provisions to address current changes in the labour force, current factors of regional differences in the country. There is really no reason why we should offer the same level of benefits in an area where they have virtually full employment as we offer to an area in which there is less opportunity to find jobs. We know that in some areas of the country people can find work if they wish to. Again, this introduces an element of fairness.
I could speak longer on this topic, Mr. Speaker. I wish I had the opportunity. Maybe I will get that later tonight, but in the meantime I thank you for the time allotted to me and I will complete my remarks another day.

We are horrified by the images of the poor and the homeless in Canada. We are horrified by the images of people lining up at food banks in our society. Over the past decades, we have made a conscious and a committed decision to ensure an economically viable means of support for all Canadians.

There are times when a person suddenly loses his or her job, and it can be for a variety of reasons. It can be for a simple reason, such as incompatibility with the workplace. It can be for reasons that are more repugnant than these. It can be because an employee must quit her job because she has been sexually harassed by her employer. In my riding of New Westminster-Burnaby these changes will have a big impact on the health of my community. Many of the jobs in my riding are dependent on the resource sector. It is important to cushion the lives of these workers during the boom and bust cycles. Right now people work 10 weeks in order to receive unemployment benefits. That is not a lot of time. Are we getting to maternity benefits now?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to continue the debate on Bill C-21, regarding the Government's proposed changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act. We in this country are faced with a
Unemployment Insurance Act
monstrous deficit. In times such as this what is required of the Government is responsible restraint.
What is required, especially now, is for the Government to strike a balance between what we must do and what we can afford to do. While this is anything but easy, it is the responsibility of this Government to address the realities of our current situation.
These proposals are a good attempt to reflect the balance which is required at this point in time. They address the limitations which our deficit has placed upon us, but more important these proposals ensure the system continues to provide assistance to those who are in need.
These proposals, in many ways, have sought to improve the current system without losing sight of the fact that we are faced with a deficit of crippling proportions. The time has come for us to try to accomplish more for less. Only in this way can we address all of our responsibilities.
The origins of our unemployment insurance system can be traced back to the period immediately following the Second World War. Faced with the possible spectre of severe unemployment, the Government of the day devised a system which ensured that the basic needs of the returning soldiers would be met. The seeds for what we have today were planted in 1971 when the system was reorganized.
We must ask ourselves, has it gone beyond what it was intended to do? Can it be improved? Can the unemployment insurance system do more to help those who are truly in need?
Can the system continue to support those who need it without serving to some as a disincentive to get back to work? Of course, unemployed workers should continue to receive benefits, but the system must be flexible enough to assist them in getting work.
There are many who want to work but, through no fault of their own, find themselves without jobs. The spirit of the Act is to support people while they look for work and to assist people with special problems so that they too can obtain work.
There are abuses of the system. The people who abuse the system are not dishonest. The truth is the system allows for, and in many cases, encourages these abuses to take place. We all know people who do not feel like

Unemployment Insurance Act
returning to work because they are entitled to more weeks of benefits. Many people do not have any objections to spending the summer collecting unemployment insurance. I think people realize this.
Never in the history of mankind have changes to society been more dramatic than they are now. The new legislation addresses the unemployment problems which are the result of this changing world: a world which finds women re-entering the workforce, a world which finds older workers displaced by changing job requirements, younger workers trying to crack the workforce, seasonal workers in and out of jobs and those facing the toughest challenge of all, the long-term unemployed.
Let us discuss for a moment the federal Government's new labour force development strategy announced in April. This will build on the success of the Canadian Jobs Strategy, and in consultation with business, labour and the provinces will provide new ways of responding to the needs of the Canadian labour market in this changing world.
Let us take, for example, the plight of many older workers. I meet many who want jobs while travelling in my riding of Elk Island. These people are accustomed to work. In fact, their pride demands that they put in an honest day's work. These older workers will benefit from the $100 million earmarked to retrain them.
For those who are in danger of losing their jobs, the new industrial adjustment service will be doubled to $30 million to help retrain workers who might otherwise be laid off. These are commonsense ideas which prevent workers from being displaced, which identify the special concerns of the older worker or those who are without skills.
I would like to speak for just a moment about young people. I have four children. How this country competes on the world stage in the future depends on how well they are prepared to meet the challenges. Support will be quadrupled through co-operative education, providing high school and college students with valuable hands on experience. Over the next four years, it will rise to $34 million. Many young people making the transition from school to the labour force will benefit from the new entry level training programs. One hundred million dollars will
be spent on this and up to 50,000 new workers will receive assistance from this program.
Forty-five million dollars will go to unemployed Canadians for increased self-employment, so that they can set up their own businesses and create more jobs. This lump sum form of benefits will also allow workers to move if they wish to seek jobs somewhere else.
This is not all. A national skills development advisory board will be set up to tell the Government what the private sector is looking for. Human resource planning will receive $65 million to further develop a national job strategy. This will expand Employment and Immigration's current human resource services. It will help industries and occupational associations plan for changes in their personal needs, using EIC programs and services. To further strengthen this plan, money will go to building networks of industry associations, unions and training institutions so they can work toward building more jobs for Canadians.
The Labour Force Development Strategy also proposes to make the system fairer by including these benefit provisions: Special unemployment benefits which will include 15 weeks of maternity benefits, 10 weeks of parental benefits and 15 weeks of sickness benefits. This will cost $450 million annually.
The system must be fine-tuned so it works best for those who need it most. We must ensure the system continues to help those who are in need, while recognizing the need for fiscal restraint. We must try to accomplish more for the people the system was originally designed for. We must try to make the system better. This is why the proposed changes are in line with regional disparities. Where there is high unemployment, people will not have to wait as long to collect benefits. They will also be able to collect for longer periods.
Seasonal workers will be helped under the proposed changes too. The Government proposes to eliminate the repeater clause. A seasonal worker who is forced to collect a second time in a year will not need to have the extra weeks of work the second time. These measures simply reflect the reality that it is tougher to find a job in the interior of B.C. than it is in southern Ontario. If we really are going to get more for less we must simply make the system work better. One way of getting more for less is by enlisting the support of industry. Since industry, both large and small, provides these jobs we must match its need for skilled labour with the need people have to

work. Instead of mobilizing a huge government bureaucracy to take care of this retraining, why not let industry experts do this? Compared with other industrialized countries, our industrial training programs lag far behind.
The Government's objective is to stimulate an additional private sector effort of $1.5 billion per year by the year 1994. This will bring the total to approximately $3 billion per year by 1994, a level which would take us up to par with industry training programs in the United States. This will help Canadians who are unemployed, Canadian who face unemployment because their skills are becoming obsolete, young Canadians who are beginning their careers, Canadians who will be helped to escape the prospect of long-term unemployment and Canadians who want to work.

The intention of these proposals is to improve the UI system while keeping in mind the necessity of restraint. These proposals represent a creative way of achieving

both. These proposals do not lose sight of our responsibilities to unemployed Canadians. These proposals are designed to provide jobs.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to participate in this very important debate on this very important Bill C-21, which amends the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is an important debate taking place here today because this Bill, which is badly flawed and unacceptable on its own for many reasons, most of which we have already heard throughout this debate, is even more repugnant when one looks at the backdrop of events that have taken place prior to the introduction of these changes.

Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), the Minister for International Trade said as eloquently as he possibly can, as all Newfoundlanders do: "Unemployment benefits are safe with the Conservatives". She stated in this House, as many other other members of the front bench opposite did at the time, that the changes were consistent with the statement that had been made by the Minister for International Trade during the election campaign.

Since the election, the Tories have come into this House and talked about the great commitments toward national reconciliation, wealth creation, job creation, and economic prosperity which they would inflict upon Canadians.
There are a number of programs which Canadians have come to respect and expect, especially from our neck of the woods in Atlantic Canada. Initially these were called regional development agreements. Then the name was changed to the general development agreements. This was a method by which the federal Government took the vast resources of this country and redistributed them, took the concept of equalization, that it did not matter where you lived in this great nation, you had a right to expect and enjoy a certain standard of living. The GDAs did this. The ERDA process which replaced it in 1984 did it. That process took money from the wealthiest parts of the country and redistributed it to places like Atlantic Canada.
During that same election campaign in November, 1988, members of this Government seeking re-election and election went on and said: "Regional development programs are safe. That is a sacred trust". Well those GDAs and subsequently the ERDAs contributed billions of dollars toward the economy of Atlantic Canada. On March 31 of this year, the Government, under its true agenda, allowed $721 million in general development agreements or ERDA agreements to expire in Atlantic
Canada alone. It is telling that the Government hid the details of this of this for as long as it possibly could.
Then there was a leak in the press and the Government had to come clean with the Canadian public. The Minister opposite from my home province, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. MacKay) who is responsible for ACOA, would shake his head many times. He should have been hanging his head in shame because he allowed his colleagues in Cabinet to take $721 million in very necessary investment in Atlantic Canada and shuffle it off under the guise of deficit reduction. That is shameful.
By March of next year, if this pattern of uncaring, this true Tory agenda, continues unabated, there will be $1,221 billion worth of development agreements that may not be renewed. An Hon. Member opposite is shaking his head. He should talk to the Premiers of Newfoundland, P.E.I. and New Brunswick who are on bended knees asking the Government to honour its commitments to Atlantic Canada and to renew those agreements that have been allowed to lapse.
Mrs. Sparrow. What about Hibernia?

He says that they may reprofile the moneys. I think we should reprofile the Minister. We should put him back on his woodlot in

Pictou County. He is not doing his job on behalf of the people of Atlantic Canada.
The tourism sector of Atlantic Canada is one of the industrial sectors that has the potential for true growth, the creation of thousands of jobs and new wealth in Atlantic Canada. That was recognized by this Government, by previous Governments and by all the Governments of Atlantic Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate this evening. I was interested in some of the comments of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Dartmouth (Mr. MacDonald), on the other side of the House.
We certainly do realize that there are areas within the regions of Canada that have more difficulties than other areas. That is exactly what the Government has been striving to overcome in the past four years.
Atlantic Canada has had the greatest economy during the past four years since World War II. Over the past four years there have been 108,000 new jobs created on the East Coast. Since we came into Government the unemployment rate has fallen in P.E.I. from 13.8 per cent to 11 per cent; in Nova Scotia it has fallen from 13 per cent to 9 per cent; in New Brunswick it has fallen

from 14 per cent to 10 per cent; and in Newfoundland it has fallen from 24 per cent to 13.5 per cent.
In 1984 the Liberal Government that was then in power put $185 million into Atlantic Canada for regional development. This year the Progressive Conservative Government will be contributing $420 million. That is almost three times the amount that the Liberals put in. Equalization payments are up 40 per cent in Atlantic Canada. Over the past four years, we have increased equalization payments by 40 per cent.
There are other areas in Canada that also have difficulties, it is not only Atlantic Canada. I want to tell Members what we have done in western Canada. In August, 1987, we developed the Western Diversification Fund. This Government set aside $1.2 billion to be used for diversification. Up until today, we have approved 1,006 projects for a total of $574 million. That is going into Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia.
When?

They started at Christmastime in 1987, nearly two complete years ago. It is continuous and extremely successful.
In 1984, when we came into power the unemployment rate in my Province of Alberta was 13 per cent. Today it is down to 8 per cent. We have created 70,000 new jobs in the Province of Alberta, and I am proud of that.
There are also areas such as the Husky upgrader where we are investing moneys to refine heavy oil so we can then ship it as light crude either to eastern Canada or to the United States. We are also putting funding into the OSLO area in which we will be able to utilize the oil sands in regard to security of supply.
Over the past four years, CIDA contract awards going into my Province of Alberta have more than doubled. Procurement contracts that we never had before we are now starting to receive. We are now building the infrastructure so that we in western Canada can also participate.
It is a privilege for me to speak on Bill C-21, a Bill that provides statutory authority for the implementation of certain provisions of the federal Government's labour force development strategy. I was reviewing the labour force development strategy and how we are reinforcing

June 21, 1989
Unemployment Insurance Act
private sector training through human resource planning and training. We are putting in an increase of $65 million to expand the current services. Obviously, as science and technology change, and as our jobs and our goals change, we have to develop the human resources.
For entry level skills development, there is an additional $100 million for training, including a new program to meet the needs of growing industries, especially those in the service sector. It is very interesting how we note that the service sector will be far more important in the years to come. For too long we in this country have rested on our laurels. We have been a resource driven country. Canadians have developed and depended upon their resources to maintain and improve their standard of living. We have oil and gas in the province from which I come and also a great deal of coal. In Canada there is a great deal of nickel, gold and iron ore. There is uranium in the Province of Saskatchewan. Of course, there are fish on the east and west coasts which, too, are natural resources. Our forestry areas also represent a tremendous resource.
In Canada we have been doing so well that we have not been looking ahead at how we will meet the markets as far as efficiency and global trading in the next decade are concerned. I guess what I could say is that we have not been sharpening our wits. We have to change our habits. Changing our habits is as important as changing the UI program and setting aside funding to retrain people so that they can meet the demands of the next decade. In this way we can go into the 21st century competing with our colleagues, not just those south of the border but those internationally.
We have to change our habits. We have to re-educate ourselves and change our direction. As I said, the best way to change our direction is through training. That must be the main way.
Another interesting development that has happened over the past few weeks is in terms of Bill C-3, which had to do with the development of the new Department of Industry, Science and Technology. We can see that the Progressive Conservative Government along with our Minister of Industry, Science and Technology (Mr. Andre) and the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Winegard), who is in the House tonight, are very much aware of how much science and technology, and research and development mean to the future development of our country. I do not know whether the Minister has ever said this, but I think he means that they are probably the weapons that will maintain and improve our economy. The Minister would very much like to see alliances formed with the Government, universities and industries right across Canada, working together to spend better what moneys we have. We are under deficit reduction. All of us on this side of the House realize how important it is to bring down the deficit and, indeed, the debt. It is not "our problem", it is everybody's problem. We do not want to be spending today, putting that on the backs of the youth of tomorrow.
In terms of initiatives to help the unemployed and in terms of training for the unemployed we have increased funds to $350 million under Section 26. The Government will consult. It will consult with the private sector and with the provinces on how best to implement this proposal. This is something we have been doing over the past four and one-half years. Instead of making unilateral decisions, national reconciliation and co-operation with all levels of Government, be they our provincial counterparts or municipal counterparts, are very important. I was pleased to hear the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) say that she will work with these particular areas.
Through employment assistance in the Canada Centres for Employment we will offer more intensive assistance to unemployed workers by directing job seekers to the services that they need and at an earlier age in an area of unemployment. There will also be help for social assistance recipients. There will be an additional $100 million made available which is contingent, of course, upon matching allocations from the provinces.
There will be help for displaced and older workers to the tune of $100 million. This money will be for special measures to assist displaced and older workers to re-establish themselves in the labour force.
In terms of self-employment, entrepreneurship and mobility assistance there is a provision for $45 million for UI recipients to capitalize benefits in one lump sum. This money could be used for start-up costs, subject to a viable business plan, or for mobility assistance up to a maximum of $10,000. This is exactly the way we should go in terms of assisting people in different regions of our country who are at different levels of employment,

people with disabilities and people who have to move in order to obtain jobs.
When this country of ours was created geologically some of the regions received some resources which turned into tremendous wealth benefits. Other regions did not receive any. Therefore people have to go to where the jobs are. We will tiy to assist them in every way that we possibly can.
As I said, I am very pleased to speak on this Bill that improves the unemployment insurance program. As Members of the Elouse are aware, these adjustments are an integral part of the Labour Force Development Strategy. This strategy signals the Government's determination to help Canadians, both employed and unemployed, as well as to help Canadians adapt to a changing labour market. Fundamental to making the transition is mobilizing and preparing our human resources.
It has been estimated that by the year 2000 almost 80 per cent of Canadian jobs will demand professional, white collar skills, compared to today's figure of 40 per cent. The traditional blue collar job is disappearing. Even those people on the shop floor are now being expected to have reading, writing and numerical skills to deal with the complex, high-tech machinery around them. We have seen that over the past five to ten years cash registers which have been computerized and which provide stock taking as well. It certainly makes conducting inventory a lot easier. However, again, we recognize that people working in the retail area will have to be better educated and better trained. That is why the thrust of this strategy is to improve the amount and quality of training and, in the private sector, to help Canadians attain skills in demand. In this regard the co-operation of business, labour and Government is essential.
Through this strategy we are encouraging the private sector to take on a leadership role in training, as the private sector has done in many other countries. The example in many other countries has proven that businesses must constantly help their workers to upgrade their skills in order to keep their businesses competitive. For instance, 1987 figures show that while U.S. firms spent about $30 billion annually on formal training and
Unemployment Insurance Act
retraining, the Canadian private sector devoted only $1.5 billion a year to skill development activities. Adjusting for the relative size of our economies and differences in survey design, the result is indisputable that Canadian firms spend barely one-half of what their American counterparts commit to improving the skills of then-employees. Herein lies the rub. We certainly have to call upon the private sector to partake in more of the retraining and, indeed, in the cost of retraining people, for people are the greatest resource of the country.
As we move into the next decade and the next century it is up to all of us, not just to the Government, to be retraining our best resources. We have to do better if we are going to be successful and compete in the international market. In this way we can ensure that Canadians will continue to enjoy one of the highest standards of living in the world.
Almost 50 years ago, when Mackenzie King's Government passed the first Unemployment Insurance Act, the intention of UI programs was to encourage industrial stability and social security. Today, the purpose of unemployment insurance programs is the same. The goal of our Government is still to protect people out of work and to maintain economic stability.
In 1989, however, the structure of the labour market is changing before our eyes. No longer does our economy depend almost entirely on a resource based industry. No longer does a high school education ensure a young person a good job.
If Canada is to keep up with the pace of expanding global markets and world competition, it is imperative that we prepare for it now. It is evident that our unemployment insurance programs, while continuing to protect workers, must evolve with the times. The Labour Force Development Strategy means a shift toward programs and services that in the future will help Canadians get back to work as quickly as possible. Clearly, training and other active employment programs are the key to preparing Canadians for the future and, to that end, the Labour Force Development Strategy outlined a wide range of initiatives designed to help these people get back to work.

Unemployment Insurance Act
Some of these programs which I outlined earlier include entry levels skill development programs, human resource planning and training programs, the Industrial Adjustment Service Program, Community Futures. These are initiatives to help the unemployed. These are all very meaningful ways that we will assist people get back to work as quickly as possible.
The amendments in Bill C-21 give effect to these changes and will see the resources committed under the UI program for active assistance increased from $405 million available today to more than three times that, an estimated $1.4 billion in the first full implementation year. These funds will be used to train and provide financial assistance to help UI claimants get job training, experience, or work.
Since 1977, some unemployment insurance money was used to provide training for those receiving benefits. Last year, for example, 74,000 claimants were trained under Section 61 programs.
The Labour Force Development Strategy proposes to extend training to an additional 60,000 trainees. Funds will be earmarked for skills training and education upgrading for displaced and older workers. This strategy recognizes that training involves much more than school costs.
Government programming has long ensured that adequate income support is available to those who need training but encounter financial barriers related to dependants, care or travel and commuter costs. We will also be making funds available for relocation assistance for an expected 5,000 claimants so those who want to travel out of town to look for work or those who want to move where job prospects are better will have income support available.
The Bill also considers those claimants who want to start a business. Assistance will be available to support the entrepreneurial ideas of those on unemployment insurance. As well, some UI funds have been set aside to provide incentives to the unemployed to find work quickly. This may be in the form of bonuses or temporary earning supplements.
Forty-nine years ago the Unemployment Insurance Act was passed to help workers in a changing labour market. Today, market transformation is again our impetus for amending the Unemployment Insurance Act. Providing a safety net for unemployed workers remains paramount. The unemployment insurance program continues to be an integral part of Canada's social system.
The size of the over-all UI program will not change. What is different is the direction of our unemployment insurance program.
Out in the domain of the unemployed, life is getting more difficult and the strategy is based on the principle that a more pro-active approach is needed by business, by government and by labour to address these needs. Clearly, the positive steps we are talking about today address the needs of workers and of the market. This will ensure Canada's prosperity tomorrow.
