Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity this evening to take part in the debate on Bill C-21.

Bill C-21 should be renamed the Tory broken promises Bill, because it implements once more the exact opposite of what the Conservatives promised the electorate during the last election campaign.
Lest one thinks that I am merely making a partisan remark, let me remind Members opposite what the Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) said during the last election campaign.
On October 14, 1988, as quoted by the Evening Telegram of St. John's Newfoundland, the Minister for International Trade said: "No one is planning any changes in the unemployment insurance program. There hasn't been any change proposed to us since we dealt with the Forget Commission and we are not contemplating any changes".
Of course, one has to bear in mind that this particular statement was made by a Tory. When quotes are made by Tories, sometimes one has to interpret them as being exactly the opposite of what was said. As Winston Churchill once put it: "The opposite to the truth was never stated with greater accuracy".
The Tories have been reducing funding for job development since they came to power.
That is not true.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
A Tory Member across the way is shouting that is not true. The Tories have reduced funding to the tune of $700 million. Now it is claiming that it is contributing $800 million, but that is almost the amount it took out. Furthermore, this does not take into account the fact that the $800 million they are contribut-
June 21, 1989

ing is being taken from the funds of the workers. They are taking it out of the UI fund.
The Member across says that is not true. Let me give her a few examples of what is happening in my constituency this year. I ask those Members to pay close attention. In the great constituency of the Glengarry- Prescott-Russell here in eastern Ontario we had a job re-entry project in Rockland, Ontario and one in Haw-kesbury, Ontario. This year they applied for four smaller programs under job re-entry.
For those people who may be listening to this debate, the job entry and job re-entry programs are designed with a particular emphasis on women who have not been in the workforce for some time or who have never formed part of the so-called active workforce. It is designed to give them skills to find a job.
Those programs in my constituency have a success rate of 90 per cent to 100 per cent. The program at the high school in Vankleek Hill had a placement rate of 100 per cent. Every woman who started the program finished and got a job. I congratulate the people who put this program together for my constituency.
This year we applied for four smaller programs totalling slightly more than what was applied for last year. Three of those programs have been refused because of lack of funding. That is the kind of commitment we see from the Tories who say that they want to train workers in order to get jobs.
About a month ago the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) sent us a large press kit inviting us to inform the population of our ridings about the great new co-op program with the schools. The very same day that I received this press kit on my desk I received a refusal from the same Minister for one of those co-op grants. It is the only one for which we applied in the constituency that I represent. That is the Government's commitment to the riding that I represent to assist toward retraining and the training of people to find productive jobs.
Let us look at what the Conservatives have done for the great region of eastern Ontario. There is a misconception that just because Toronto is doing veiy well economically, all of Ontario does extremely well and
Unemployment Insurance Act
there is no such thing as unemployment in our great province.
That is not true. For instance, the riding I represent in Prescott County has an unemployment rate that nears 14 per cent. That is only about 60 miles from Parliament Hill where we are standing right now. The unemployment rate in my area is very high.
I think I heard someone across the way suggest: "Why don't they get a job?" That is very typical of the sensitive Tories. It is surprising that they got 19 per cent of the votes last time in my riding with that kind of a mentality. That is all they received and it is about 15 per cent more than they deserve.
Let me read from the Throne Speech wherein in indicated:
The new federal approach to regional development is working.
That is very debatable. The Throne Speech of April 3 continued:
Decentralized decision making, through the regional agencies in Western Canada, Northern Ontario and Atlantic Canada, has been instrumental in stimulating both entrepreneurial endeavour and business investment. It is important that we talk about the sweeping changes announced on April 11 which we are debating tonight. The strategy includes massive cuts to UI regular benefits, an expansion of UI training benefits, a new 10-week parental benefit, the stacking of sickness, pregnancy and parental benefits, and an expanded role for labour and business in labour adjustment.
Clearly the most important feature of the Government's strategy is the proposed massive cuts to regular UI benefits. Regular UI benefits account for 86 per cent of the $10.9 billion in UI benefits claimed last year. The Government has estimated that the new benefit structure will cost $1.3 billion from regular UI benefits. Workers will not only bear the cost of UI changes in reduced benefits, but beginning January 1, 1990 the entire cost of UI benefits will be financed from worker and employer premiums. Worker premiums will be increased from the current level of $1.95 per $100 of weekly earnings to $2.25 per $100 of weekly earnings to replace the nearly $3 billion per year which the Government contributes, or did in the past, for regionally extended benefits. The 15 per cent increase in worker UI benefits will cost a worker making $400 a week $62.40 in increased UI premiums.
The Government will also increase the penalties for fraud by workers or employers. There are about 200 fraud cases a year out of 3.2 million claimants. This is clearly part of the Government's broader strategy to create public hostility toward UI and UI claimants. The Government's justification for massive cuts in basic benefits is to reallocate 10 per cent, or $1.3 billion, of UI
June 21, 1989

funds to training and to cover charter cases; $750 million to training; and $500 million to cover the Charter cases which the Government lost.
The cuts in regular UI benefits are not necessary to finance those changes to UI. At the current premium rate of $1.95 per $100 earned, UI premiums would generate $900 million more than the expenses currently charged to premiums. Had the 1988 rate of $2.35 remained in effect this excess or surplus would have amounted to $4 billion. Premiums could still have been substantially reduced while providing improved special benefits and better training coverage for UI claimants.
Certainly it could have happened if the Government had not chosen with the introduction of this Bill to opt out of unemployment insurance. A feature of the Government's strategy is to shift the cost and burden of unemployment and adjustment to workers, including unemployed workers. In shifting the burden, the power of employers will be increased in shaping conditions of work and wages. A more subtle aspect of the strategy is to highlight penalties of voluntary quits to create a public impression that unemployment is voluntary and to whip up public hostility to the program.
The proposed restructuring of regular UI benefits threatens the viability of UI as a social insurance program for which it was founded. Millions of workers will be required to pay premiums to a plan in which they will never be eligible to receive benefits because of the increase in required weeks to qualify. Workers who most need the benefits for a long duration will have their benefits terminated prematurely.
For example, older workers, to whom the Member from Calgary referred, who have very long spells of unemployment will have little protection because of the very sharp reduction in the duration of weeks of benefits. Well over half the claimants who qualify for UI will have their maximum weeks of entitlement reduced by 13 weeks.
The 1971 Unemployment Insurance Act struck a difficult but workable balance in sharing the burden for unemployment among workers, employers, and the Government. This balance was reflected in the UI benefit structure and in the formula for financing those benefits.
Unemployment Insurance Act
The current benefit structure has three phases. The first two phases relate benefits to a claimant's weeks of work. When I say "current", I am talking about the one we are about to vote out of existence tonight by the other side of the House. The third phase extends UI benefits by two weeks for each half point the regional unemployment rate is above 4 per cent. The three-phase structure worked and worked well.
The over-all maximum duration is 52 weeks less a two-week waiting period. The maximum duration of benefits for most workers in the 48 UI regions has been 40 weeks to 52 weeks over the past 15 years because the unemployment rate in veiy region except two, Toronto and Kitchener, in recent years has been well above 4 per cent. Currently, as of March 1989, the entrance requirement in 22 regions is only 10 weeks for the same reason. The regional unemployment rate has been very high through the 1980s.
Under the new program, in Mission-Coquitlam, my riding where unemployment is 9.8 per cent, the number of weeks needed to qualify will go from 10 weeks to 16 weeks, a 60 per cent increase in the entrance requirement.
In addition to increasing the entrance requirement, the Government is reducing the duration of benefits. The duration of benefits will still vary with the regional rate of unemployment. Under the current system, a worker with 15 weeks living in Mission-Coquitlam, for example where the unemployment rate is between 9 per cent and 10 per cent, could collect 39 weeks of UI benefits.
The same worker, under the proposed system, does not even qualify. Sixteen weeks would be required. If the worker is able to get an extra week to qualify, the maximum weeks of benefits under the Government's proposed system is 27 weeks, 20 weeks less than the current system. A worker in Mission-Coquitlam at the current regional unemployment rate with 52 weeks of work, under the proposed system, I repeat, is limited to 49 weeks, one week less than the 50 weeks under the current system.
The closest we have come to defining a full employment measure in any Canadian statute is the 4 per cent unemployment rate used in the Unemployment Insur-

ance Act to determine the number of weeks UI benefits should be extended as unemployment increases.

That is the Tory plan.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you for giving me an opportunity to speak in this debate on Bill C-21, the Conservative Government's mean-spirited and ill-conceived reform of our unemployment insurance system.
During the 1988 election campaign, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) said that his Government was not planning nor contemplating any changes to Canada's Unemployment Insurance Act. The Minister said one thing and his Government did another. The list of broken promises keeps getting longer and longer.
The purpose of the Bill we are debating today is to cut back our unemployment insurance system drastically. The Government's proposed reforms are designed to place the entire burden of Canada's $12.6 billion unemployment insurance program squarely on the shoulders of this country's employees and employers.
Both labour and business groups have predicted that the inevitable result of this Bill will be higher unemployment. Nowhere will this effect be felt more strongly than in Atlantic Canada. It stands to reason that in times of austerity or economic downturn employers will think twice before hiring workers if they are forced to contribute a greater amount of money to unemployment insurance.
The Government plans to turn its back on the workers of Canada. Its arguments for doing so do not stand up to the crucible of careful analysis and reason. The first argument used to justify this reform is the alleged necessity of reducing the deficit. All this rhetoric about deficits plaguing the Canadian economy is just a smoke and mirror screen used by the Government to hide its true agenda, which is to cut social spending. Economists do not even agree among themselves as to whether or not the deficit and debt constitute a serious problem for our country. Moreover, a careful study of history tells us

June 21, 1989
Unemployment Insurance Act
that our country in the past lived with high deficits and high ratios of debt to gross domestic product.
The second most obvious reason for the Government's introduction of the legislation is that as part of its delivery system for the Free Trade Agreement it has given in to the Americans who believe that our unemployment insurance system constitutes an unfair trading practice and that it should, therefore, be curtailed if not completely eliminated.
We of the Liberal Party warned Canadians during the last election that the Conservatives would dismantle the essential public services in this country for the sake of free trade. The Government's actions have confirmed our dire warnings. It has cut regional development grants, unemployment insurance tonight, provincial transfer payments, grain transportation subsidies, CBC funding, VIA Rail, and the list goes on and on. The Government made cuts to social programs as well as to a variety of other services in order to create conditions which would permit American businesses to compete with their Canadian counterparts on what the Conservatives call a level playing field. If a level playing field means plant closings and hundreds of people thrown out of work, including 975 workers at Northern Telecom in Aylmer, Quebec, 139 workers at Pittsburgh Paints, 600 Gillette Canada employees in Quebec and Ontario, then I would suggest the Government has succeeded very well indeed.
What Canada needs right now to deal with all the lay-offs caused by free trade is a more progressive and compassionate unemployment system. Instead, the Government tables this legislation which makes it more difficult for displaced workers to obtain unemployment benefits. Where is the logic in all of this, Mr. Speaker?
The third excuse which the Government uses to denigrate Canada's unemployment insurance system is that it believes workers to be fundamentally la2y and that a progressive unemployment insurance system encourages this nasty tendency. For anybody with at least a modicum of common sense and understanding of human behaviour, this argument is nothing more than vapid rhetoric. Individuals take pride in and get satisfaction from gainful employment. People use unemployment insurance benefits out of necessity, not choice. If the
Tory Government does not understand this, then it had better do some more homework.
Statistics show us that only an infinitely small percentage of unemployment insurance claimants either cheat or abuse the system. According to figures supplied by the Department of Employment and Immigration, only 5,507 people were caught cheating in 1987-1988. During the same period, 6,215 people refused a job while receiving unemployment insurance benefits and thereby lost their rights to the benefits.
If you tally up these figures, the number of people who either cheated or refused a job while claiming benefits is negligible. Only 0.45 per cent of all claimants can be said to have abused the system. Think of it, Mr. Speaker, that is less than 1/2 of 1 per cent of the 2.4 million people on unemployment insurance. If the Government thinks a progressive unemployment system encourages laziness, then I would have to say that the Government's thinking is muddleheaded because figures do not lie.
There is absolutely no relationship between a progressive unemployment insurance system and a high level of abuse and cheating. In fact, countries which have the most progressive unemployment systems, as the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) said in this House on June 6, have the lowest rates of unemployment in the world. For example, Sweden, Switzerland, West Germany, France and Australia all have unemployment rates of less than 5 per cent. Moreover, the average rate of unemployment in Canada between 1965 and 1980 was 5.6 per cent, a very low figure indeed. Therefore, it is a fallacy to assert that a progressive unemployment insurance system encourages sloth.

Mr. Speaker, the Unemployment Insurance Act was brought in by Mackenzie King's Liberal Government in 1940, following the great economic crisis of the 1930s. The basic purpose of this law was to ensure that all Canadians could meet their essential needs when they were laid off against their will. Unemployment insurance is only one of the features that makes our society more compassionate and fairer.
The Bill that we are debating today is clearly contrary to the spirit of that law. The Government intends to reduce its contributions to the Unemployment Insurance Program by $1.3 billion. Furthermore, it will use this money to offset the cuts of over $700 million that it made
June 21, 1989

in the last five years. Instead of using funds from general revenue, the Government will take this money from the Unemployment Insurance Fund. From now on, all workers will have to pay for the special training programs.
Mr. Speaker, we completely agree with the principle that the unemployed should have access to better training programs. Nevertheless, the Government should not take money from the Unemployment Insurance Fund to finance these programs.
The present Unemployment Insurance Act provides that 2 per cent of the Fund is to be used to finance special training programs. With the reforms proposed by the Government, the main burden of financing these programs will fall on the Unemployment Insurance Fund. This is a regressive tax. Everyone will lose: workers who receive training, companies hiring the workers so trained, and the economy which benefits from these new skills.
A crucial problem arising from this ill-conceived reform is that the Government can give people in regions of high economic disparity no assurance that they will benefit from this training. Will New Brunswickers who receive high technology training be able to work in their province or will they have to move to Montreal, Toronto or Vancouver?
Mr. Speaker, I get tired of hearing the Government say that it is creating all sorts of economic opportunities while the Atlantic provinces are getting a very raw deal. The Government is closing military bases, abandoning rural post offices, thumbing its nose at regional development agreements and drastically slashing VIA Rail's budget. This Government is deliberately laying off hundreds of workers and it has the nerve to say that it is contributing to this region's economic development. To top it all, the Government is limiting access to benefits.
To set the record straight, Mr. Speaker, unemployment in the Atlantic region remains much higher than the national average. Many of our young people must leave this region if they want to have interesting careers. I know that this suits the Conservatives very well. But

the people of the Atlantic provinces want this exodus to stop.

Members that in the 15 years prior to the recession, under a Liberal Government, the average unemployment rate was 5.6 per cent?
The rate of unemployment in Atlantic Canada is staggering. For all their fine promises, the Tories have let Atlantic Canada down. The Government's proposals for reform are terribly short-sighted. It has increased the number of weeks needed to qualify because it believes that work, any work, is easily available. I hate to break it to the Government, but that is simply not the case for Atlantic Canada. In many instances, work is seasonal and when it runs out, there are only two alternatives, unemployment insurance or welfare.
The changes proposed by the Government will be devastating to the Atlantic region. Failure to obtain the number of weeks needed to qualify for unemployment insurance will mean that many people will be forced on to the provincial welfare rolls. That is not a very pleasant prospect, I assure Hon. Members.
The unemployment rate in the riding of Restigouche, which I represent, is 15.6 per cent, nearly twice the national average. Under the current system, people need 10 weeks of work in order to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits. The duration of benefits is a period of 42 weeks. Moreover, the penalty for people who quit without proper reason is six weeks. The revisions the Conservatives are proposing will considerably alter the system. The duration of benefits will be reduced by five

weeks, from 42 to 37 weeks. Finally, the penalty period for people who leave their jobs without proper reason will be 12 weeks.
The Government tells us that its reforms will benefit workers. What effrontery. Will workers benefit from longer qualification periods, shorter durations of benefits and training for jobs that do not exist? Certainly not.

Unless the Government is going to create an environment in which there are opportunities, then people will not work, and certainly small business needs opportunities. Small business often works on a low-profit margin and works long hours. Small business is the industry in this country which is creating jobs, they are the ones who should be having some advantages.
We are waiting, Mr. Speaker. We hope that the Government will take some direction regarding our motion with respect to the Federal Business Development Bank. We are still waiting. We are not holding our breath but we are waiting.
In the meantime, what has this Party done to small business? It has introduced an unemployment insurance Bill and budget cuts which are going to directly affect small businesses. We have heard all sorts of speeches and all sorts of very valid comments about the effect that this Bill will have on the workers in this country and about the disadvantaged in this country. Certainly small business fits into that category.
This is a Bill which is going to put the burden of social programs directly on the backs of workers and small business employers. That is a sad comment to make in this day and age. This is a government which is cutting some $3 billion that it took from general revenue to put into the unemployment insurance program. That is

where the money should be coming from. It was a distribution of income and funds which were transferred more equitably across this nation. That is now gone.
Small business will not notice it immediately because the unemployment fund has a surplus. That is simply because the rates were increased last fall. The Government will say that it is throwing hundreds of millions of dollars of new funds into job creation. These are neither new funds, nor are they for the benefit of small business. The Minister of Finance removed these funds from the unemployment insurance program-when he brought down his Budget. Small business is not in a position to take advantage of those programs. If this Government would like to do something for small business, then it should be acting in a manner which is going to be responsible to small business. It should consider passing legislation that is going to allow small business to survive in this country. It should be creating an environment whereby small business can function. It should be using the Federal Business Development Bank to provide loans to small business. It should be having an unemployment insurance program whereby the employer is not burdened with carrying the weight of the social programs on their backs. This program affects dramatically the very regions of our country. This is not unlike other Bills this Government is passing. Certainly there have been tremendous cuts in provincial transfer payments. There have been tremendous cuts with respect to regional programs.
There have been base closures. The base closures alone are a disgrace. The Government has closed the base at Summerside in Prince Edward Island which employed some 1,100 people. These are 1,100 direct jobs lost in a city of some 8,000. That is going to be devastating for that community.

This Bill affects the regions of this country. It affects Atlantic Canada. It affects northern Ontario and northern Quebec. It affects western Canada. They have all suffered under this Government. This is a Government which is failing to regard the welfare and the needs of this country.

June 21, 1989
Unemployment Insurance Act
I am truly sad to be in the House this evening because we will be voting on second reading of this Bill in a very short time and unfortunately, with a majority government on the opposite side, we are going to lose this vote.
Canadians will long remember this. Canadians will not forget this. Certainly we on this side of the House will do our best to remind Canadians of the dastardly approach and the dastardly deeds which this Government is perpetrating on this nation.

Mr. Speaker, we are very fortunate to live in this high-tech era. We can enjoy wonders of technological ingenuity today that were inconceivable even to the last generation.
Personal computers, VCRs, word processors; all of these conveniences have become part of our daily existence. They are the result of technology which was non-existent 30 years ago.
This technology is enhancing our personal, lives but it is also affecting us in the workplace. Canadian workers must meet an unprecedented demand for skills. That demand will only increase in the years ahead.
That is why I support this legislation to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act. Bill C-21 is a major component of the Government's Labour Force Development Strategy. The key to this strategy is that it will help train Canadians in the skills they need now and in the future.
Bill C-21 has three objectives. The first is to prepare Canadian workers for existing and future labour market challenges. The second is to right some longstanding wrongs by ensuring that the Act meets the Government's commitment to employment equity and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The third is to ensure that UI benefits are improved and preserved for those who need them most.
I would like to concentrate my remarks on that third area, Mr. Speaker. This legislation proposes fundamental changes to the UI program which affect the amount of time people must work to qualify for UI benefits and how long benefits will last. It also introduces new control measures. Canada is a very generous country. This generosity extends to its social programs, including
unemployment insurance. As it now stands people need only work 10 to 14 weeks to qualify for benefits depending on the local unemployment rate. These entrance requirements are among the lowest in the world. In Japan and France people must work 26 weeks during the previous year in order to qualify. But the generosity can sometimes have detrimental repercussions.
As a Member of Parliament in my riding of Simcoe Centre many constituents often tell me that this is the case with the UI program, that our UI system is a disincentive to work. Many people believe that UI encourages some people to work just long enough to qualify for assistance who then quit and collect benefits for up to a year. Now I know that the vast majority of Canadians do not fall into this category and I would never imply that they do. But it is an irrefutable fact that some people are trying to take advantage of this system and those that do think that they are beating it.
We are proposing to increase the number of weeks of employment needed to qualify for UI in most areas of the country based on a local unemployment rate. My constituents in Simcoe Centre believe this is a very reasonable approach. This means, for example, that people living in communities where unemployment is at 6 per cent will need to work 20 weeks to qualify for UI instead of the current 14 weeks. At the same time the Bill remains sensitive to the needs of those people in areas of high unemployment. People living in areas where the unemployment rate is more than 15 per cent will need only ten weeks to qualify. Where the unemployment rate is 10 per cent only 16 weeks is needed to qualify.
For seasonal workers these new provisions may sound threatening. Let me assure them that they have no reason to be concerned. You see, Mr. Speaker, seasonal workers by the very nature of their employment often collect UI twice within the same 52-week period. A current clause in the Act requires people who have already collected benefits within the past year to work from 16 to 20 weeks in order to qualify again. This is six weeks more than when they first qualify. This is known as the repeater clause. It was an onerous condition for seasonal workers and we are now eliminating it entirely. This means that seasonal workers will, generally speaking, now find it easier to qualify for UI.
June 21, 1989

This move will of course simplify administration of the UI program and as you can imagine anything that simplifies the complex administrative structure of a program like UI is welcomed by everyone involved. In fact, this legislation contains other measures that will make the program run more smoothly. One of them involves calculating the duration of benefits. The present method used to determine how long people will receive benefits is a very complicated three phase system based on a week's work and the local unemployment rate.
The proposed legislation fortunately will streamline this progress. It continues to base the duration of benefits on the number of weeks worked and the local unemployment rate but it eliminates that three phase complexify and substitutes it with a straightforward table.
We have also made necessary adjustments to the number of weeks people can collect benefits. These adjustments are again dictated by the unemployment rates in different areas. A person in Barrie where prospects abound should not need to collect UI benefits for 50 weeks. Someone on Cape Breton Island where opportunities are limited is entitled to as much income support as possible.
As well, the Government is proposing measures to deal with people who quit their jobs without just cause. It may surprise you to know that more than a billion dollars is paid out every year to people who quit their jobs without just cause. Obviously we must do something about this. The legislation deals with people who quit their jobs voluntarily, who are fired for misconduct or refuse to take a job. Under current legislation these people lose their benefits for six weeks. Under Bill C-21 they stand to lose them for between seven and 12 weeks. When they begin or resume collecting benefits they will also find their benefit rate lowered from 60 per cent of their weekly insurable earnings to 50 per cent. I think it is veiy appropriate that I bring up EIC at this time. As you know EICs, Canada Employment Centres, have an exemplary record in finding jobs for people and people for jobs. In my riding the staff work diligently to provide guidance and to arrange interviews and training course for clients.
Some clients do not take advantage of these opportunities and those who do not will find their benefits cut off for one to six weeks under the legislation. I must also tell you that people who find jobs before their disqualification period is up may receive a surprise if he or she
Unemployment Insurance Act
collects UI down the road. The Bill also allows for any weeks of a disqualification period not served because work was found to be carried over to any future benefit period over the next six years.
Let me add that these disqualification periods may be deferred if the claimant is eligible for sickness, maternity or parental benefits. Let me also make it clear that people who quit their jobs for valid reasons such as hazardous working conditions or harassment will not be subject to these penalties.
We are also introducing new measures to discourage UI fraud. It is a matter of opinion but perhaps the worse abuse of the UI program is perpetrated by those who knowingly give false information. Unfortunately it is a fact of life and it must be dealt with. Under the Bill, employers who submit false employment information will now be penalized up to nine times the maximum benefit they pay weekly. Also anyone penalized for minor infractions can have the penalties deducted from future benefits they receive over the next six years.
As you know, people who commit major acts of UI fraud are subject to prosecution. In the past anyone convicted of the crime received a maximum $500 fine, six months in jail or both. The new legislation raises the fine to a much stiffer maximum of $2,000. These are necessary measures which will serve to make the UI program fairer and more efficient. Instituting these measures will free up $1.3 billion that will be rechannelled directly into the UI program in ways that I have indicated before. It will help thousands of Canadians who are willing to work. That is what the labour force development strategy is all about.
I have just outlined the benefit structure and control measures proposed in Bill C-21. We hope to implement the new legislation early in 1990. Only then will the funds for training programs and the new charter improvements be accessible. I trust that my colleagues in the House and the Members of that other place will give it full and due consideration.

Mr. Speaker, during the election campaign, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said, "We shall maintain all our social programs without fail." At the same time, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) promised that there would not be any changes to the unemployment insurance system. Let me read an October 14,1988, article in

the St. John's, Newfoundland newspaper, The Evening Telegram:
Changes in UI Program? 'Nonsense', retorts Crosbie.
The federal government has no plans to make changes to the unemployment insurance program, Hade Minister John Crosbie said Thursday.

"You're damn right I asked him (prime minister) about it.
Once again, there is another broken Tory promise. The Government has broken its promises and has cut back on unemployment insurance benefits.

They have been cut back. The Government is using this money to replenish the programs it cut back over the last five years by $700 million. Rather than using funds from general revenue as is normally the case, the Government is taking it away from the unemployed. I call this shameful.
This means that all workers will pay for training without any assurance that they themselves will benefit from that training. It means that labour-intensive industries will subsidize training for high-tech industries which are often capital intensive. It means that low-paid service workers will help pay for the training of high paid-high tech workers.
The Government is hypocritically using the pretext of adjustment to finance its deficit reduction plan at the expense of unemployed Canadians. The Prime Minister and his Government are taking away $2 billion from unemployed Canadians. While the unemployment insurance expenditure reduction will be effective almost
immediately, the entry level training program will be phased in over a four-year period.
Under the present unemployment insurance program, workers in firms pay into a fund knowing that money will come back to them in the form of benefits if they become unemployed, sick or pregnant. Now, under this proposal, they have no assurance that money will be paid back or that any money will come back to them at all.
According to the program, for example, $230 million will go for training activities in the private sector. Part of this money, $65 million, is for human resource planning. This is a good thing and one wonders why it has not been going on over the last four or five years. Once again, money will be used from the unemployment insurance fund, money that was available for workers when they were laid off, to pay for the human resource planning.
A strong labour force development strategy depends on a sound full employment policy that supports research and development, post-secondary education and literacy initiatives. The more basic education a person has, the easier it is to train him or her. That is just common sense. Given that, in the near future, almost half the new jobs will require more than five years of combined education and training beyond the completion of high school. The Government should be developing a comprehensive full employment policy and increasing, not decreasing, its support for research and development, post-secondary education and literacy.
The Government has announced new training initiatives without consulting with the provinces and without any kind of mechanism to monitor this training. Without such consultation, the Government cannot satisfy Canadians that the training programs will meet the needs of the economy and that the quality and standards of the training will be high enough to meet the challenge.
The Government is shifting the financial burden to the provinces. This is clear throughout this Bill. The provinces will be required to extend their work projects in order for workers to become eligible for unemployment insurance benefits or will need to extend social assistance to those unable to find additional work to qualify for unemployment insurance. In either case, the prov-
June 21, 1989

inces are faced with additional expenditures without any prior warning.
The federal Government has yet to make available impact studies which would indicate the number of workers who will be adversely affected by these changes. It is no wonder. I believe that the numbers would be staggering.
Already, British Columbia and Quebec have acknowledged that the changes could result in increased social assistance costs. Mr. Buchanan from the Province of Nova Scotia has said that this will definitely increase his province's costs.
The changes to unemployment insurance will adversely affect the rural Canadian economy. Let us take, for instance, my riding of Haldimand-Norfolk. There are towns in my riding in which the unemployment rate is staggering. It is nothing like the southwestern Ontario unemployment rate of somewhere in the neighbourhood of 8 per cent. There are places in my riding with unemployment rates of anywhere between 15 per cent and 20 per cent. Under this Bill, my riding is considered to be part of the Niagara Peninsula so the number of weeks required for eligibility will be increased. That is shameful and nowhere in this Bill is this problem addressed.
These additional wages that firms will pay because of this Bill will increase their costs, and as a result will increase the cost to consumers. These firms will be less competitive as well. If they compete on the international market, firms could suffer economically because of these increased costs.
Unemployment insurance benefits have always served as a stabilizer in communities where there is high unemployment. Unemployment insurance benefits stimulate local economies and keep local businesses alive. A reduction in these benefits will adversely affect local businesses and entire local economies.
While training is a good thing in itself, one cannot train someone for a job that does not exist. Often in rural communities, there is one industry. Alternatives are not available. If these people get trained, they will have to move out of the regions to find employment. The Government has chosen to increase mobility funds to help workers move to areas where there are employment opportunities rather than to create a comprehensive regional development policy. As my friend from Dartmouth said today, the Government is asking people to move west or to Toronto, to move where the jobs are, instead of bringing in creative, innovative programs
Unemployment Insurance Act
which will help address the needs of the unemployed. The Government should have examined the entire unemployment insurance program in depth and considered changes in the context of comprehensive income security instead of adopting such punitive measures.
On page 30 of the budget papers, the Government stated that it will continue to contribute to the financing of programs in difficult economic times when it is inappropriate to raise premiums and prudent to allow deficits to build in the unemployment insurance account. We should not have to point out to the Government that we are in poor economic times now and that to aggravate the situation, the Government is shirking its responsibilities by absolving itself from contributing its share to unemployment insurance benefits.
Let us examine current employee-employer contributions and then compare them with the changes announced in the Budget. Currently employees pay $1.95 per $100 of insurable earnings to a maximum of $11.80 per week. Currently, employers pay $2.73 per $100 of insurable earnings to a maximum of $16.52 per week.
As of January 1990, the Government will no longer contribute to the unemployment insurance fund. Employees and employers will pay extra to cover the increased costs. In 1990, employee contributions will increase to $2.25 per $100 of insurable earnings to a maximum weekly contribution of $14.29. This maximum weekly contribution is $2.49 more than employees are currently paying or $129.48 more per year.
In 1990, employer contributions will increase to $3.15 per $100 of insurable earnings to a maximum weekly contribution of $3.48 more than employers are currently paying or $180.96 more per year. We know who is paying for the mismanagement of the economy over the last few years. It is the employers and the workers of the country, and that is shameful.
Let us analyse the situation in light of the new changes. The premiums paid by employees and employers have increased substantially. The Government points out that the increase from $1.95 to $2.25 per $100 of insurable earnings is still lower than the rate employees paid in previous years. That is true. It was $2.35 over $100 of insurable earnings paid in 1985, 1986, 1987, and 1988. However, the Government has failed to show that it has also substantially increased the maximum weekly insurable earnings so that the maximum weekly contribution by employees will increase substantially. This is shame-

Unemployment Insurance Act
ful.. Employees will now be paying almost $130 more per year in unemployment insurance premiums.
The Government predicts that the cost of its unemployment insurance expenditures for 1989 will amount to approximately $2.9 billion. By abdicating its responsibility to pay unemployment insurance contributions, the Government is forcing $1.2 billion in additional premiums to be paid by employees, and $1.7 billion in additional premiums to be paid by employers. By eliminating its contribution, the Government has stated to people in regions most in need, and particularly to fishermen, that it can no longer contribute to their well-being. The Government has cut adrift those most in need.
My friend, the Hon. Member for Dartmouth (Mr. MacDonald) explained that quite adequately in his speech earlier. I thought it was a wonderful speech, and one of the best that we have heard in the House on this matter.
During the 1988 election campaign, Tory Members of Parliament went across the country and stated that social programs would not be affected, that free trade would have no effect on our social programs or on our unemployment insurance program. We have seen the results. This Government brought in a program which, quite frankly, I believe was made up by the Minister for International Trade at the whim of the Americans who stated that we could not have government contributions to the unemployment insurance system in Canada. The Minister for International Trade said: "Yes, Sir, Mr. President". Once the Government had made all those promises, the promises are broken.
Employees will now pay higher premiums and receive benefits for a shorter duration. Typically, with the Government it is now pay more for less. It is Tory math.
Ordinary Canadians cannot afford this increased burden. Those Canadians earning less than $30,000 a year paid 58 per cent of all employee premiums in 1986. Those earning $50,000 to $100,000 paid only 7 per cent of all employee premiums in 1986. Is that what the Government calls fair? I do not call it fair. Again, the Government is reducing the deficit on the backs of those least
able to pay, and on the backs of those regions less able to vote in the number of Members that will help defeat the Government. That is Toryism. The Government picks on eastern and rural Canada. Those people will be most affected by this program.
The unemployment system is regressive by nature. In 1990, the premiums are capped when income reaches $33,020. Even with this range, the tax is not progressive, since it is set at a flat rate.
Instead of increasing the rates on low and middle-income workers, the Government could have funded the unemployment insurance program by removing the cap on the premium rate, so that a person making $100,000 would pay $2,250 a year in premiums instead of the current $784. We believe that a person who makes $100,000 should not only have to pay $784 as a maximum premium.
Where will corporations get the money to pay the tax? From reducing payments to shareholders? Not likely. Raising prices and getting it from customers, or cutting costs and getting it from employees seems more realistic. Those in the weakest economic position will bear most of this tax. Of almost $7 billion of tax increases, including the unemployment insurance changes, less than $1.5 billion are progressive. The rest are regressive, and sometimes seriously so.
The Government and the Prime Minister have termed social programs as a sacred trust. The Prime Minister has now reneged on his word with a brutal attack on the unemployment insurance system. It has taken $1.3 billion from the unemployment insurance fund and has not said how many workers will be affected. We have not seen any studies. I doubt if the Government knows what the studies show. In fact, I do not know if the Government has conducted any studies. Perhaps the Government is hiding them.
How many will lose benefits? How many will go without unemployment insurance? The Government has not stated what regions of the country will be hint the most.

It is interesting to note that between 1984 and 1989 employment and training programs were cut by some 30 per cent by the Government, from $2.2 billion in 1984 when the Liberals left power, to $1.5 billion in 1989. That is a reduction of some $700 million.
On April 11, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) announced that she was putting $800 million back into the program, almost the same amount that the Government had taken out. We have yet to see a penny. The Government is fixing a problem that it created in the first place.
Time after time Members of the House have heard petitions from one coast to the other that we ought not to proceed with the proposed changes to the unemployment insurance fund which will disentitle up to one million Canadians from receiving unemployment insurance benefits.
Canadians are opposed to the so-called harmonization of unemployment insurance to conform with the Free Trade Agreement. This will destroy the historic role of unemployment insurance in this nation. Our system is the envy of many countries around the world, including the United States. The present Government is dismantling the foundation of our social structure which was built upon a sacred trust.
Canadians will not forget what the Government is doing. Next time at the polls, Canadians will not let the Government forget what it has done to them.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise this evening to speak on this most important piece of legislation.
Last fall, as I campaigned throughout my riding of Macleod, people frequently asked me: "When is the Government going to do something to reform the unemployment insurance system?" I am proud to be able to say to my constituents in Lundbreck, Pincher Creek, Vulcan, and other communities that the Government has taken positive, concrete, and well-considered steps to change the UI system to make it more responsive to the real needs of Canadians.
Bill C-21 in a very progressive way changes the nature of our unemployment system. Now, unemployment insurance will be used to train and prepare workers for a job. As the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) stated: "The best social program is a job". My constitu-
Unemployment Insurance Act
ents and I fundamentally believe that this is an essential principle.
The world is changing. I know Members and colleagues opposite do not like to admit that, but we are entering a time of truly global change.
We are entering a truly global economy and Canada's workforce must be prepared to meet those challenges. In coming years Canada is going to require a highly skilled workforce. We are going to need a well trained and highly productive labour force if Canada is to achieve her rightful place in the global economy.
My constituents recognize that we need a better educated work force and more skilled employees. However, according to a study performed by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business last year, almost one-half, about 43 per cent of Canada's small businesses complain that they cannot find appropriately skilled help. Indeed, Canada currently spends half as much on training and skill development per capita than does the United States. We cannot allow this situation to continue. We must begin a vigorous program to educate and help Canadians train themselves so that we can compete with the rest of the world.
Bill C-21 goes a long way toward addressing this very serious problem. Currently only 2 per cent of UI expenditures are on training Canadians and preparing them to find a job. This Bill proposes to shift the spending priorities of the UI fund to direct up to 15 per cent of spending to preparing Canada's labour force, giving individual Canadians the chance to learn, to build their future through training and skill development. That is for moms, dads, sons, and daughters. I think that is a very positive initiative.
Indeed, through our labour force development strategy the Government will work with and stimulate the private sector to double its commitment to training from $1.4 billion to nearly $3 billion by 1994. That is double the investment in Canadians, double the investment in skills. That is a real commitment to people.
We are talking here about reallocating UI funds. We are talking about renewing Canada's priorities and looking to the future. I know that my colleagues opposite do not always like to look to the future. They like to paint a much more bleak future. We are talking about preparing

June 21, 1989
Unemployment Insurance Act
Canadians for the challenges that a competitive workforce is going to create.
This Government is not creating that international competition. It is simply allowing Canadians the opportunity to respond to the pressures which we face internationally.
This Bill proposes to change the schedule of benefits under UI to make it more responsive to varying regional unemployment rates. Not only will this legislation achieve this goal, but it will also free up resources within the UI fund to be spent on training. Almost $1.3 billion will be redirected toward training, providing benefits to older Canadians, and increasing maternity or parental benefits. I am sure all Members of the House will agree that these are important and laudable goals.
At present, once an employee reaches the age of 65 he or she is no longer eligible for assistance from the UI fund. Indeed, if an employee turns 65 while collecting benefits, those benefits are immediately cut off. My constituents have expressed to me that they found the situation intolerable. I am pleased to see this Bill before the House since this unfair and previously discriminatory provision in the UI system will finally be removed. This Bill will extend UI coverage to older Canadians who choose to delay their retirement.
More than this, the changes as a result of this Bill to the UI system will enable the Government to develop a $100 million program to help displaced older workers. We will be assisting older Canadians to advance their skills, to retrain, and, if necessary, to upgrade their education.
I cannot stress enough how important this issue is. I have talked to constituents on the streets of High River and other communities in southern Alberta. I cannot count the number of people who have mentioned the special difficulty faced by older Canadians seeking work. This is a very fair, compassionate and practical measure.
This Bill will also provide much needed assistance to Canadian families. These are challenging times in which to raise children. I know that the Government should continue to provide support to Canadian families. Changes to our tax system have allowed parents more flexibility in choosing how to care for their children. This Bill and the changes it will bring to the UI system reflect
the Government's continuing commitment to help strengthen Canadian families.
A full $450 million has been earmarked for maternity or parental benefits. Like other initiatives the Government has taken, parents will have more flexibility in how they choose to care for their new-born baby. Canadian families will be able to count on having as much as 30 weeks of UI benefits to help them through the financial struggle of having a child. It will also provide more flexibility to the system so that potentially both parents will have an opportunity to be with their youngster during those exciting first few weeks.
What a joke!

My colleague mentions jokes. I note this for interest because colleagues opposite talk of how reallocating UI funds is not acceptable to them. It is nothing new. The Opposition which today is so strongly against this idea are members of the Party which was involved in changing the allocation of UI funds in the first place.
Let us go back to 1976. The Minister of Manpower, Bud Cullen, said: "Amendments will also allow us to take a more positive approach to unemployment through resource allocation. It will permit experimentation with the use of unemployment insurance funds for programs of training, work sharing, and job creation". Today, the crowd opposite tries to oppose these very kinds of principles. It is remarkable.
I turn my attention to another important aspect. As part of this Government's efforts to assist areas experiencing unreasonably high unemployment, the Community Futures Program was developed. In my riding of Macleod, just as one example, there are areas, as there are in other parts of the country, in real need of economic development and diversification. The Government has made long-term substantial commitments to provide assistance to these areas.
For example, in the Crowsnest Pass, which includes a number of communities, the Government has committed over $2 million to the Business Development Centre of the Crowsnest Pass Economic Development Board.
The Government has also committed $400,000, approximately, to the Crowsnest Pass through the SelfEmployment Incentive Program, a very practical
June 21, 1989

program designed to help unemployed workers test new business ideas.
In the northern end of my riding, the Highwood Economic Development Corporation, which serves the Municipal District of Foothills as well as the County of Vulcan, is administering and investing $1.9 million over five years from the Community Futures Program. These programs are providing realistic responses to genuine needs.
The Government has renewed and invigorated its commitment to the Community Futures Program. The changes we are proposing to the unemployment insurance system will result in an extra $50 million every year for the Community Futures Program. This will ensure that this very important program will continue to provide areas of higher unemployment with assistance to diversify and develop their own economies.
I know how important this program has been in my own riding. I am sure that all Members of the House are pleased that the Community Futures Program will now have more resources.
I confess, my constituents have often told me that they feel the UI system is being abused. This is regrettable. They feel cheated and angry when they see some Canadians quitting their jobs without just cause and taking advantage of UI benefits.

speechtext: I know it is the summer solstice and I realize that this will be the longest day. I hope we could get finished without getting too warm in this Chamber. The Hon. Member for Macleod has the floor for another nine minutes.

This may be the longest day, but this will not be the longest speech.
It is regrettable that Canadians should feel cheated and angry when they see others taking advantage of the
Unemployment Insurance Act
system. I think the people of Macleod are justified in getting angry.
This Bill will amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to make it more difficult and less tempting for people to take advantage of the system.
Less tempting?

The Bill proposes that workers who voluntarily quit their jobs will not only have their benefits delayed, but they will also receive a reduction in the over-all level of benefits. As a result of this Bill, people seeking to take advantage of the unemployment insurance system will be disqualified from receiving benefits from seven to twelve weeks. Once their disqualification is over, they will receive benefits of only 50 per cent of their insurable earnings.
This Bill also substantially increases the penalties for both employers and employees who try to defraud the UI fund. This is as it should be.
When the unemployment insurance system was set up in the 1940s, it was designed to provide temporary assistance to unemployed workers. The UI fund was not created to replace other forms of social assistance. It was created to assist workers in getting through tough times of unemployment. This Bill represents a return to some of the fundamentals of the unemployment insurance system, and the people of Macleod whom I represent are pleased that these changes are taking place. They are pleased that there will be less abuse of the system. They look forward to the training programs, the economic development programs, and the maternity parental benefits provided by this Bill.
They are pleased that the UI system will no longer discriminate against older Canadians. They are glad that the Government has had the guts to undertake these reforms and start to put the UI fund to work for all Canadians.
The people of Macleod firmly support this important initiative of the Government. The Government is taking positive steps with these unemployment insurance changes. We are talking about investing in individuals. We are talking about investing in moms, dads, sons, and daughters. We are talking about Canadians who have aspirations to get ahead and use their own strengths to earn a living and meet their own challenges by investing in themselves to make a constructive and a real contribution to Canadian society.

If Canadians seize this opportunity and take up this challenge, the result will be that all Canadians will share in a greater wealth and a stronger future.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to debate the Bill before the House of Commons today. It is with great sorrow that I witness one of the cornerstones of Canada's social fabric dismantled, or should I say destroyed, by the Conservative Government. It is painfully clear that the purpose of Bill C-21 is to cut back radically on Canada's unemployment insurance system and, in effect, privatize our oldest social program which has served Canadians well since 1940.
One must not forget that the UI system was brought into being as as result of the devastating effects of the Great Depression of the 1930s on our society, to ensure that no Canadian would have to suffer such hardship ever again.
It is because of this compassion toward the human condition that Prime Minister Mackenzie King instituted this national insurance scheme. Unemployment insurance was brought into being to make absolutely certain that no one would starve, lose their home or loved one as a result of losing a job. This deep caring for humanity is deeply embedded in the Liberal Party tradition.

It would be wrong to say that we in the Liberal Party do not want the Act changed, amended or improved. In fact, Mr. Speaker, in 1955 and 1971, under Liberal Governments, amendments were made to bring this legislation up to date with the needs of the time.
However, Mr. Speaker, that is not what this Bill proposes. As presented by the Minister of Employment and Immigration, this BUI threatens one of the main pUlars of this country's social security network. Indeed, the Minister dares to go ahead with this Bill, even after she claimed in the last election campaign that if she and her party were returned to power, no social program would be privatized.
Mr. Speaker, it is really a shame that Canadians have been misled by this Minister and her party, and I can assure you that next time, they wUl not be fooled.

MUlions of Canadians are asking themselves why the Government has decided to go back on its election promises. People are asking themselves why Canada's sacred trust has lost its sanctity with the Progressive Conservative Party.
In my opinion and that of my Party, there are three reasons why the Government has adopted this policy. The first reason is rather clear, given the contents of the Minister of Finance's leaky Budget. In an inappropriate manner, the Government is using the proposed BUI C-21 as a means of cutting Canada's national debt, 50 per cent of which was accumulated during the time the Conservatives have been in power. That is a fact Members opposite would conveniently like to forget.
We have frequently seen the Government's total lack of caring or understanding of average Canadians. The provisions of this BUI are the worst example of that fact. What the Minister is doing, along with her colleagues in Cabinet, is attempting to cut the deficit on the backs of the unemployed. Instead of strengthening the Canadian unemployment insurance system, the Government is cutting its commitment in a futUe deficit reduction exercise. Instead of choosing a more logical means of cutting the deficit, such as taxing profitable corporations and cutting back on waste and inefficiency of government, the Minister is attacking those Canadians who have the least to offer.
The Minister is taking the money that would have gone to pay for the rent, food, and other basic necessities and allocating it for training programs. I would have been supportive of the creation of new skill training programs, but not at the expense of funds that are supposed to help people survive whUe looking for employment.
It is a strange set of priorities that the Minister is displaying. Instead of understanding the cyclical nature of poverty and the fact that basic assistance is needed to sustain life whUe individuals are unemployed, she is offering obscure and abstract training programs that wUl some day enable people to sustain themselves. What these people need is assistance to get by untU they can find real jobs with real potential.
June 21, 1989

The second reason this Government brought forward this Bill has unfortunately become too clear following its election. Undeniably, Bill C-21 is a first step leading to a plan for the giants of the business world to move to free trade. By withdrawing from the unemployment insurance program, the Canadian Government is doing what the American Government wants, because the U.S. Government will not be able to take reprisals against us on the pretext that Canada uses unemployment insurance to subsidize its workers.

The Bill will be even more damaging when considering it in the light of free trade. By pulling out of UI, the Government of Canada has asked Canadian workers and employers to fill the $3 billion void caused by its absence.
This will result in either a higher unemployment rate, caused by employers reluctant to pay this hidden payroll tax, or it will lead to a powerful lobbying effort on the part of big business to be exempt from paying the unemployment insurance premiums because of their need to have a balanced playing field with their United States counterparts.
While corporations get larger and more profitable, average Canadians have to pay the price in terms of wages and social insurance. Knowing how close big business is with the Conservative Party, one can only wonder how long it will be before unemployed Canadian workers will be asked to foot the entire bill for unemployment insurance.
The last reason the Government has decided to implement this new unemployment insurance policy is its misguided Conservative ideology. Unfortunately, the majority of the Members opposite believe that a caring and compassionate social welfare system will lead to a greater degree of laziness. This archaic view of individuals who must take advantage of various social schemes is reprehensible in a country like Canada.
The majority of Canadians are tired of listening to the rantings of the dinosaur club and its talk of welfare bums when the actual number of people abusing the system is far below levels articulated by Members of the Government.
Unemployment Insurance Act
The statistics speak for themselves. The number of individuals caught cheating on the unemployment insurance was 5,507 out of 2.4 million Canadians who use the UI system. This represents only 0.2 per cent of the total number of Canadians who use the system. This is to edify the Hon. Member for South Shore.
Only 6,215 people have refused jobs found for them through UI. This represents only 0.25 per cent. Both these categories together represent less than half a percentage point of all individuals using the system. Despite this fact, the Conservative Government is still intent on characterizing by its statement that abuse is rampant in the system all people dependent on government assistance as ungrateful welfare bums.
That ideological bend is a major force behind this Government's withdrawal from unemployment insurance and a strong motivater for the severity of this Budget. This Government should learn from international examples that progressive unemployment insurance schemes go hand in hand with low unemployment rates. Social democratic countries such as Sweden, Austria, and Switzerland have some of the most progressive UI plans in the world and an unemployment rate below 5 per cent.
In fact, the average unemployment rate in Canada during the 15 years of Liberal Government preceding the global recession was 5.6 per cent. That puts into real perspective the fact that the Conservatives have not been able to bring the unemployment rate below 7 per cent once in the five years they have been in power. So much for the Government's record. The only place in Canada where full employment exists is in the overheated economy of Metropolitan Toronto.
It seems that this Government would be more than pleased if people from Comer Brook and Sydney moved to Halifax. They would be more than pleased if people from the Gaspe and the Saguenay moved to Montreal. The provisions of this Bill will make staying in the economically depressed regions of the country even more difficult.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration has stated that Bill C-21 still maintains the regional sensitivities to allow people from remote areas of Canada to stay in their homes. This is simple nonsense. If we look at the figures, we can see that in every region of the country the requirements for eligibility have increased. Also, the Tory Government seems to be sending an odd signal. In previous years, in an area of low unemployment, one needed 14 weeks to qualify for benefits. Now 14 weeks will qualify one only in regions where the unemployment

Unemployment Insurance Act
rate is between 11 per cent and 12 per cent. How absolutely scandalous. Instead of facilitating an easy transition back into the workforce, the Tories are going to penalize you if you do not take the first employment opportunity that comes your way. It does not matter if you are a skilled professional, the Conservative Party would rather see you flipping hamburgers than looking that little bit extra longer for work that will lead you to a career in which you will be best able to contribute to Canadian society.
When is this Government going to create those jobs that will help sustain families at a decent level, instead of perpetuating their misfortune and increasing the number of working poor?

Now see how Bill C-21 will affect Quebec. Under the present system, Quebecers paid $2.5 billion in premiums and collected $3.3 billion. Obviously, on looking at these figures, we must revise and improve this program. By withdrawing from the unemployment insurance program, the Government is forcing employers with a large labour force to make up the difference.
In Quebec, this will mean $100 million more will have to be spent by the Government, given the large number of employed workers.
Mr. Speaker, again, taxpayers, particularly those in Quebec, will pay the bill for the lack of federal financial assistance in this area. All employers in Quebec will have to pay more, to compensate for the measures in the Bill.

No matter which way we look at it this is a bad government policy. By shortening the number of weeks for benefits and increasing the necessary time for people to qualify, the Conservatives are offering Canadians more options.
When benefits are cut and the person is still unemployed, he or she will either have to go on provincially funded welfare programs or join the increasing number of Canadians who must rely on bread lines and soup
kitchens for food and shelter. Unfortunately, that is going to be the legacy of the Conservative Government.
I know that Members opposite are going to claim that I am against job training programs. Nothing could be further from the truth. Liberals are not opposed to job training. In fact, from 1984 to 1989 the Tories have cut the funds for training programs from $2.2 billion to $1.5 billion. It is only now that they have taken from the funds designed to pay for the necessities of life that the training spending is back to its original level. As a concerned citizen I find this option most regrettable.
In an interview the Minister for International Trade said last October that the Government had no intention of cutting the unemployment insurance system. He even told the press that the Prime Minister was in full agreement with this position. I would like to know from the Hon. Minister what has changed between then and now to prompt such a devastating attack on our social programs.
It is obvious that the Conservatives have broken yet another of their election commitments. Might I add that Canadians will not forgive them again. The people of this country are tired of listening to the empty rhetoric of this Government. Canadian people need a Government that cares about their needs and is willing to respond not merely through words but through actions.
Bill C-21, if passed, will be disastrous for Canada. It will contribute to a greater division between the rich and the poor and will lead to a tremendous burden on our provinces. It creates a situation in which government is withdrawing from UI and, by doing so, privatizing one of the most important aspects of Canada's social security network.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, and I conclude on this point, the only recourse, the last resort for Canadians will be welfare. It is scandalous, Mr. Speaker, to force people to such a solution!

Mr. Speaker, we are here tonight to debate Bill C-21, an Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Employment and Immigration Department and Com-
June 21, 1989

mission Act. First reading of the Bill was on June 1 of this year. We in the New Democratic Party oppose this Bill and will oppose it with all that we have throughout this debate and for as long as we can. Of course tonight closure has been imposed and in just a few hours we will be voting on second reading of the Bill.
The Government has introduced what I believe to be two very important and negative pieces of legislation since I was elected on November 21. The first of those important and negative pieces of legislation was the Bill to implement the free trade deal. I remember standing in this House about nine o'clock on one of those evenings before Christmas speaking to a lot of Canadians who I know were not watching because of the time of day. Once again I find the same thing on a very important piece of legislation affecting a great number of people. I am standing here in the House late at night debating something that the people of Canada should be hearing during the normal course of the business day.
I am very happy to be talking about this Bill because there are a lot of things that I think need to be changed which are not addressed in this piece of legislation. I am a veiy active Member of Parliament. I have a lot of contact with my constituents. I deal with their cases on a very personal basis, be it unemployment insurance, immigration, visa matters or even social assistance cases. I am more than happy to sit down in my office and help them through their problems.
I have dealt with quite a few people who have difficulty with the unemployment insurance program. I have a lot of contact with the unemployment insurance offices in my riding, one in North Battleford and one in Meadow Lake, Saskatchewan. The people who work in those offices are very dedicated individuals working hard to administer a very difficult and flawed program. This legislation is going to make their job much more difficult, and it is going to make the people they are dealing with much more angry.
I have listened to quite a number of speeches tonight from government Members who have talked about the need to change the legislation because of the way in which the current system is being abused. I have heard Members on this side of the House correct Members on the other side of the House by indicating that the abuse

rate of the unemployment insurance program is less than 1 per cent. I know from dealing with people in my office that the people who are having difficulty with the unemployment insurance program as it exists today are not abusing the program. They are in desperate need of the program, and they are in desperate need of improvements to the program.
I want to cite a particular case with which I am just finishing. It first came to my attention on April 27 of this year. A young woman in my riding had left her place of employment in early April. She had a veiy good reason for leaving her place of employment, but there was some difficulty in communicating that information to the people at the Canada Employment Centre who were administering the unemployment insurance program. To make matters very simple, it was a dispute with her employer.
On April 27, after a couple of weeks of receiving no satisfaction in dealing with the office and getting her claim settled, she finally achieved eligibility for benefits under the program but was disentitled in her first week of benefits because the workers at the unemployment insurance office questioned her about her child care arrangements in her family circumstances. She lives on a farm a few miles out of town and on one day she had difficulty getting a caregiver to look after her young infant when she had a job interview. Canada Employment disentitled her for benefits because, they said, she had inadequate child care arrangements. That was on April 27 when she came to see me.
After we investigated her claim and discussed it with the people at the Canada Employment Centre, she was put back on the benefit roll, but because of her disqualification she was penalized four weeks. Since she could not serve the disqualification at the same time as the disentitlement, she served the four weeks from April 28 and then had to serve another mandatory two-week waiting period, which has to be served by all UI claimants before the benefits would be paid.
If we add this up we find a young woman in an area where jobs are hard to find with a young child at home, unemployed, with no income at all for 10 weeks as a result of the problems with the existing program. She is back on benefits and she will get her first cheque on June 23. The Canada Employment Centre has recognized that
